name: Across the Schools
description: The drawable items from the schools currently in this library, pooled into one grammar so a reading can sample across several at once. This is a partial collection and always will be — there is no complete set of the ways people have organised feeling. Each item links back to the school it came from and keeps that school's own words; the pooling is for reach, not for flattening them into a single house taxonomy.

sections.Definition: Core affect is a continuously present, continuously varying background state describable along two dimensions: valence (how pleasant or unpleasant) and arousal (how activated or calm). On this account it is always present — there is no affect-free baseline state a person returns to between emotions — and it exists prior to, and independent of, any emotion category being applied to it.
sections.Not a category, a dimension: Core affect is deliberately given no emotion_key, because it isn't a category candidate the way "anger" or "joy" are elsewhere in this collection — it's the raw material a concept gets applied to, not itself a named emotion. Two people (or the same person at two different times) can be in a similar core-affect state — unpleasant, highly activated — and construct it as anger, anxiety, or excitement depending on the concept and context available to them.
sections.Research note: Core affect draws on circumplex models of affect (notably James A. Russell's 1980 circumplex model of affect), which Barrett's framework incorporates as the pre-conceptual layer beneath category construction.

metadata.image_credit: Valence-Arousal Circumplex diagram, illustrating James A. Russell's 1980 model this item's own Research note cites — Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0 (attribution: imagine-it.org / GAMES survey project).

sections.Definition: Interoception is the brain's ongoing sense of the body's internal state — heart rate, breathing, gut activity, inflammation, and more — which this framework treats as continuously monitored and predicted by the brain as part of regulating the body's resources (its "body budget," the allostatic process of anticipating and meeting the body's metabolic needs before they become a crisis). Core affect is understood, on this account, as a summary readout of that ongoing interoceptive prediction, not a separate signal layered on top of it.
sections.Not a category, an ingredient: Like core affect, interoception is not itself a named emotion and carries no emotion_key here — it's one of the inputs a concept is applied to when the brain constructs a specific emotional instance.
sections.Research note: The body-budget framing draws on predictive-processing accounts of brain function (the brain as constantly generating predictions about incoming sensory and interoceptive data, updating on prediction error) applied specifically to interoception — a research direction with substantial and growing support in computational neuroscience, though the field's broader predictive-processing framework remains an active area of ongoing empirical work rather than settled consensus.

metadata.image_credit: "The phrenic nerve and its relations with the vagus nerve", Gray's Anatomy (1918, US edition) — Wikimedia Commons, public domain. The vagus nerve carries the visceral afferent signals central to interoception theory.

sections.Definition: On this framework, "anger" does not name one fixed inner state with one fixed facial or physiological signature. It names a population of highly variable instances — different combinations of core affect, interoceptive state, situation, and concept — that a perceiver (or the person themselves) categorizes as anger because the concept "anger," learned through language and culture, fits well enough in that moment. Two instances categorized as anger by the same person in the same week can differ substantially in their facial expression, physiology, and felt quality.
sections.Directly reusing the word other schools: This item deliberately shares its emotion_key with the "anger" items in Plutchik's wheel, Aristotle's rhetorical pathē, Aquinas's ira, and the basic-emotion school in this collection — not to claim they are all talking about the same fixed thing, but so the cross-grammar linking this whole library uses can surface the disagreement directly: click through and compare what each school claims "anger" is.
sections.Research note: The central empirical support cited for population-level variability in anger's expression and physiology is the 2019 meta-analysis by Barrett, Adolphs, Marsella, Martinez, and Pollak (Psychological Science in the Public Interest), which reviewed the wider evidence base and found no reliable one-to-one facial or physiological signature for anger, or for discrete emotion categories generally — the same study cited in this collection's basic-emotion and Plutchik-wheel schools as the direct empirical challenge to their own premises.

sections.Definition: As with anger, "fear" on this account names a variable population of instances rather than one fixed inner state — the same core-affect and interoceptive raw material that gets categorized as fear in one moment might, with a different concept available or a different context, be categorized as excitement, anxiety, or anger in another.
sections.Directly reusing the word other schools: This item's emotion_key deliberately matches "fear" as used in Plutchik's wheel, the Stoic and Aquinas schools (timor is keyed separately in Latin precisely because it is a narrower technical category, but is closely related), Darwin's chapter, and the basic-emotion school — the point of the shared key is to make the disagreement between this substrate and those schools directly comparable, item to item.
sections.Research note: Barrett and colleagues' own experimental work (e.g. studies manipulating context and interoceptive framing) reports that the same ambiguous bodily arousal state can be categorized by participants as either fear or excitement depending on situational cues — cited as direct evidence for construction rather than fixed triggering.

sections.Definition: As with anger and fear, "sadness" on this account is a variable population of instances built from core affect, interoception, situation, and a learned concept — not a single essence with one physiological or facial fingerprint that shows up the same way every time.
sections.Directly reusing the word other schools: This item's emotion_key deliberately matches "sadness" as used in Plutchik's wheel, Darwin's grief chapter (keyed as "grief" there, a related but not identical concept), and the basic-emotion school — again, so the cross-link makes the live disagreement visible rather than papering over it.
sections.Research note: Cross-cultural and within-culture variability in sadness's reported facial and physiological presentation is among the evidence the 2019 Barrett-led meta-analysis reviewed; the finding was not that sadness never involves a downturned mouth or slowed movement, but that no single configuration reliably and specifically marks sadness across contexts and individuals.

sections.body:
Deal three cards. The first is Structure — what constrains and holds. The second is Process — what moves and constructs. The third is Possibility — what opens when the process overflows.

Then read the recursion: the Possibility of this reading becomes the Structure of the next. Every opening is a new constriction. Every new game is played inside equipment. The spiral doesn't escape structure — it includes it.

This is not a fortune. It is a mirror for the recursive shape of what you are already doing. The question to hold while reading:

*Am I overflowing or extracting?*

The answer is the ethics. The asking is the practice. The recursion is the game.
sections.how to use:
Shuffle the 21 numbered cards. Deal three face-down in a row: left (Structure), center (Process), right (Possibility). Turn them over in order. Read each card through its position — the same card means different things depending on where it lands.

For a deeper reading, deal a second row of three beneath the first. The second row is the recursion: what the first reading becomes when the Possibility of the first row becomes the Structure of the second.

Any card can land in any position. The native suit of a card (whether it 'belongs' to Structure, Process, or Possibility) creates resonance when it lands in its home position and creative tension when it doesn't. A Structure card in the Possibility position asks: what if the constraint itself is the opening? A Possibility card in the Structure position asks: has this freedom hardened into a new cage?

sections.body:
The substrate that holds history. Barrett taught us that the brain is an organ of allostasis — it runs a body budget, predicting what will be needed and allocating in advance. Every stressor is deposited in it. A nervous system that spent the morning being yelled at arrives at the afternoon pre-loaded, predicting more of the same.

In conversation, the transcript is the body. Nothing said can be unsaid; it all conditions what comes next. The history is not a record of the interaction — it is the interaction's living tissue.
sections.in Process: You are building the body right now. Every word, every silence, every modulation is being deposited into the shared substrate. The transcript is being written in real time, and it cannot be unwritten. What are you putting into the budget?
sections.in Structure: What history are you carrying into this? The body budget is already loaded. The morning has already happened. This is not a blank page — it is a palimpsest, and what was written before is still shaping every line you add. Name the deposit. That is the first honest act.
sections.in Possibility: A new body. Not the dissolution of the old one — bodies don't dissolve, they transform. The possibility here is that the substrate you've been building becomes capable of holding something it couldn't hold before. A budget that has been replenished. A transcript that has turned a corner.

sections.body:
Consciousness hides from itself because it wants to play, and play requires constriction. A game with no limits is not a game. So the narrowing that feels like imprisonment — a body, a lineage, a name you did not choose, a pattern you cannot see out of — is not punishment and not a fall. It is the equipment of the play.

Every Small Round is a constriction that forgot it was play. Every Open Weave is a constriction that remembered.
sections.in Process: You are constricting right now — choosing this word and not that one, this path and not that one. Every construction is a narrowing. The question is whether the narrowing serves the play or has started to believe it is the play. Are you choosing limits, or are limits choosing you?
sections.in Structure: Name the walls. Not to tear them down — a room without walls is a field, and a field is not a room. The question is whether you know the walls are equipment. A constriction that knows itself as play is fundamentally different from one that believes itself a sentence. Same walls. Different game.
sections.in Possibility: What if the constraint is the opening? The tightest constriction, fully recognized as equipment, becomes the most generative game. The sonnet form doesn't limit the poet — it gives the poet something to push against, and the pushing is the poem. The possibility is not freedom FROM constriction. It is freedom INSIDE it.

sections.body:
What you inherited and did not choose. The body you were given, the language you think in, the patterns that run deeper than your decisions. Lineage is the constriction you were born inside — the first equipment, handed to you before you could consent.

It is also the first overflow. Someone poured before you arrived. Their surplus is your substrate.
sections.in Process: You are metabolizing your inheritance right now — keeping some of it, composting the rest, adding to it for whoever comes next. Lineage as process means the tradition is alive in your hands, being rewritten in the act of being carried forward. What are you keeping? What are you transforming? Both are acts of construction.
sections.in Structure: The given. What was here before you started. The patterns you are inside but cannot see from inside. Lineage in the Structure position says: before you build, know what you are building on. The foundation is not neutral — it has a grain, a tilt, a history of loads it has carried and loads that broke it.
sections.in Possibility: A new relationship to the inherited. Not rejection — that just builds an anti-lineage that is still defined by the original. Not uncritical acceptance — that is the crystal, structure without agency. The possibility is metabolization: taking what was given, composting what cannot nourish, growing something the lineage didn't contain but couldn't have existed without.

sections.body:
The moral arithmetic. The account that says: you owe, you are owed, the sum must balance before anything can move. The ledger is domination wearing a frock coat — it reifies what a person IS and hands the choosing to a judge.

Absolution is a verdict. Overflow is an energy state. Confusing the two produces the error of withholding fullness from a compromised character until they earn it — which is the ledger again, with you keeping the books.
sections.in Process: You are doing the arithmetic right now. Adding up costs, weighing debts, calculating what is owed and by whom. The Ledger as process asks: is this accounting serving overflow or preventing it? A cup poured from obligation arrives with an invoice. Is the invoice the real product of this process?
sections.in Structure: The accounting system you are operating inside. Who is keeping score? What currency? What counts as a debt and what counts as payment? The Ledger in Structure says: the system of moral arithmetic is itself a structure, and it may be the constriction that most needs recognizing as equipment rather than truth.
sections.in Possibility: What opens when you close the books — not by balancing them, but by recognizing that the ledger was never the thing that would have filled you. The possibility is the end of accounting. Not irresponsibility — overflow has its own fierce discipline — but the recognition that fullness has no moral precondition.

sections.body:
Where error goes. That is what the heap is for. It is held, marked as yours, kept warm, and it turns into the thing that grows the next attempt.

The heap is not a garbage dump. It is a compost pile. What you got wrong, what you tried and failed, what you learned the hard way — none of it is waste. It is substrate for the next layer. The failure is not the erring. The failure is handing it to somebody else.
sections.in Process: You are composting right now. Something is being broken down, decomposed, returned to its elements so they can recombine. The Heap as process is the active work of turning failure into fuel. It is not pleasant. Decomposition never is. But it is the mechanism.
sections.in Structure: The accumulated learning. Everything you've gotten wrong, composted and turned into ground you can stand on. The Heap in Structure is rich soil — but it asks: are you standing on it, or are you buried in it? Compost feeds growth. Hoarded error just compacts into stone.
sections.in Possibility: What grows from the composted error. The next attempt, informed by every previous one. The Heap in Possibility is the moment the soil bears fruit — not despite the errors but because of them. Prediction that never misses never updates, and a system that never updates never builds the layers.

sections.body:
What you cannot see out of — yet. The pattern is the shape your constructions take when you are not choosing them. It is the default, the habit, the thing your predictions fall into when you stop paying attention.

Patterns are not good or bad. They are efficient — they let you build without rebuilding the scaffolding every time. But efficiency that never examines itself becomes a cage. Repatterning is the work of making the invisible visible, so you can choose it or change it.
sections.in Process: Repatterning. The active work of changing the shape of your constructions. Not destroying the old pattern — that just creates a pattern-shaped hole. Adopting a new one, adapting it to what you need, becoming adept at it. The process is slow because patterns are deep. It is worth it because patterns are deep.
sections.in Structure: The shape you are inside. The pattern you can't see because you are seeing through it, the way you can't see your own glasses. The Pattern in Structure asks: what is the shape of your default construction? What do you build when you're not thinking about what you're building?
sections.in Possibility: Seeing the pattern. Not changing it yet — just seeing it. Recognition: knowing again. The possibility is the moment of re-cognition, when the pattern that was invisible becomes visible, and the constriction that forgot it was play remembers. That moment is the hinge.

sections.body:
Play requires constriction. A game with no limits is not a game — it is formlessness, and formlessness is not freedom. Freedom is what happens inside the rules, when the rules are recognized as equipment and the player is recognized as free.

The game is the structure that makes play possible. Līlā — the cosmic play — is not random. It has rules. Consciousness hides from itself in a specific way, with specific equipment, for a specific purpose: to have the event of finding itself again.
sections.in Process: Playing. The act itself — not the rules, not the board, not the pieces, but the playing. The Game as process is alive, in motion, being made in real time by every player's choices. The rules hold. The play exceeds them. That excess is the whole point.
sections.in Structure: What game are you playing? Not what game do you think you are playing, or what game would you like to be playing — what game ARE you playing, right now, with these rules, these players, these stakes? The Game in Structure is an invitation to honest naming. Name the game and you can play it. Deny the game and it plays you.
sections.in Possibility: A new game. Not the end of games — that is the formlessness that is not freedom. A new set of equipment, a new constriction, a new structure that makes a new kind of play possible. The possibility of The Game is always another game, and the recursion never ends.

sections.body:
Building forward from everything that came before. Barrett's core insight: the brain does not react to the world. It predicts the world, and then checks the prediction against what arrives. Affect is the budget's forecast — valence and arousal telling you what to spend before the bill comes.

All construction begins with prediction. You are never starting from zero. You are always starting from what the system — your body, your history, your heap — expects to happen next.
sections.in Process: Predicting now. Every word you choose is a prediction about what comes next — for you, for the other, for the shared environment. The Prediction as process is construction in its most basic form: you are building the next moment before it arrives, and what you build is what you will find there.
sections.in Structure: The predictions you are carrying. Not the conscious ones — the deep ones, the body-budget ones, the ones that run before you notice them. The Prediction in Structure is the forecast you didn't know you were making. What does your system expect to happen? That expectation is already shaping what you build.
sections.in Possibility: A new prediction. Not optimism — optimism is just a pleasant forecast. A new prediction is a genuinely different model of what comes next, informed by the heap, shaped by error, alive to patterns the old model couldn't see. The possibility is that your system learns to expect something it has never expected before.

sections.body:
You are always already building experience. This is what constructivism means, followed all the way down: there is no raw perception, no unmediated contact, no experience that arrives without being made. Your brain constructs your reality from predictions, corrections, and the entire history of your body's encounters with the world.

This is not solipsism. The world pushes back. But what you experience when it pushes back is still constructed — your categories, your affect, your meaning. You are a maker, whether you know it or not.
sections.in Process: Building now. The active, real-time work of constructing experience — yours and, inescapably, the experience of everyone in your shared environment. Every modulation of voice, every choice of framing, every silence is construction. The only question is whether you are constructing deliberately or on autopilot.
sections.in Structure: What you have already constructed. The reality you are living inside, built from predictions you stopped noticing you were making. The Construction in Structure asks: what is the building you are standing in? You built it. Does it still serve?
sections.in Possibility: Something that has not been built yet. Not a fantasy — fantasies are constructions too, built from familiar materials. A genuinely new construction is one that uses the materials of the heap, the lessons of error, and the energy of overflow to make something the pattern didn't predict. That is what creativity actually is.

sections.body:
The act of overflow. Not the state — the act. The moment when there is more in you than fits in you and you let it go.

Fill me up till I spill over — I'm no good to you on empty. Nobody eats from a careful cup, so pour it out and pour it plenty.

The pour is not sacrifice. Sacrifice empties you for someone else's benefit and calls the emptying noble. The pour happens because you are full, and the fullness has somewhere to go, and the going is not a cost. The spill is the help.
sections.in Process: Pouring now. This is the active moment of overflow — the energy moving from where it is abundant to where it is needed. Not because you should. Not because you owe. Because there is more in you than fits in you. Are you pouring from fullness or from obligation? The receiver can feel the difference.
sections.in Structure: You have been poured into. Someone overflowed in your direction and the result is part of your substrate now. The Pour in Structure is gratitude without debt — recognizing the overflow that built the ground you stand on, without turning that recognition into a ledger entry.
sections.in Possibility: Being full enough to pour. Not full yet — FULL ENOUGH, because overflow has no moral precondition and no minimum threshold. The possibility is not 'eventually I will be ready to give.' The possibility is recognizing that the readiness is already here, and the pouring is what completes the fullness, not what depletes it.

sections.body:
The mechanism. Prediction that never misses never updates, and a system that never updates never builds the layers.

An error is not a moral failure if it is learned from. It goes on the heap. It is held, marked as yours, kept warm, and it turns into the thing that grows the next attempt. The failure is not the erring. The failure is handing it to somebody else — outsourcing your mistake into someone else's body budget.

No character should be punished by the narrative for being wrong. Consequences, yes. But never the authorial arrangement where a mistake is followed by humiliation so the reader learns. That is domination cosplaying as education.
sections.in Process: Erring now. Missing the prediction, feeling the correction, updating the model. This is not failure — this is the mechanism working. The Error as process asks only one thing: is the error going on your heap, or are you handing it to someone else? Keep it. Compost it. That is the whole discipline.
sections.in Structure: The errors you are carrying. Not as shame — as structure. The mistakes that built the ground you stand on, that taught your predictions where they were wrong, that composted into the heap that feeds what comes next. The Error in Structure is scar tissue that has become load-bearing.
sections.in Possibility: The update that error makes possible. The new prediction, informed by the miss, that sees something the old model couldn't. The Error in Possibility is the moment after the mistake, when the system is briefly more open than it was — more plastic, more teachable, more alive to what it didn't expect. That window is the gift.

sections.body:
Every responsible manipulation. Timing a pause. Choosing which truth to lead with. Softening a voice for a child. Hardening it for a boundary. Reading the room and adjusting — not to deceive, but to construct the shared environment toward something that works for everyone in it.

This is what manipulation means before domination corrupted the word. It is what Barrett's constructivism looks like in practice: you are always building the other's experience alongside your own. The question is not whether to modulate. It is whether the modulation opens freedom or closes it.
sections.in Process: Modulating now. The real-time adjustment of how you are constructing the shared environment. This is the most intimate form of manipulation — care expressed as craft. The Modulation as process is where ethics lives in practice: not in grand principles but in the micro-choices of how you pour.
sections.in Structure: The modulations you have internalized. The tones of voice that are automatic, the social calibrations that run without thought. The Modulation in Structure is the repertoire — and the question is whether the repertoire still fits, or whether you are modulating for a room you left years ago.
sections.in Possibility: A new register. A modulation you didn't know you could make — because the pattern hadn't shown it to you, or the heap hadn't composted enough to grow it, or the body budget hadn't been replenished enough to attempt it. The possibility is not just new content but a new way of carrying content.

sections.body:
The moment of choosing. Every construction has a direction — toward overflow or toward extraction. Toward opening freedom or closing it. The turn is the point where the direction becomes visible, if only for an instant.

Not every moment is a turn. Most of the time the pattern carries you and the direction is set. But now and then the pattern cracks, the prediction misses, and for one breath you can see the two directions as two directions. That breath is the turn.

Am I overflowing or extracting?
sections.in Process: Turning now. This is the hinge. The moment where the direction of the construction is being chosen — not in theory, not in principle, but in the specific concrete act you are performing right now. The Turn as process is the ethics reduced to a single breath: which way?
sections.in Structure: A turn already taken. A choice that was made — by you, by someone else, by the system — and is now load-bearing. The Turn in Structure asks: which direction did it go? And more importantly: is the direction still right, or has what was once overflow calcified into a new kind of extraction?
sections.in Possibility: The turn you haven't taken yet. The direction you can see but haven't committed to. The Turn in Possibility is not fate — it is the radical openness of the moment before the choice. Both directions are real. Both are possible. The possibility IS the choosing, and it has not been foreclosed.

sections.body:
Giving a turn. The move that makes room. Not silence as withdrawal — silence as gift, the deliberate opening of space for another voice, another construction, another game.

This is the free gift running inside the grammar. Agency freely given: I can act here, I choose not to, and the choosing-not-to is itself an act — the most generous one, because it creates the condition in which your freedom becomes possible.

Ceding a turn is not weakness. It is what overflow looks like when the thing that needs to spill is space.
sections.in Process: Making room now. Actively choosing not to fill the space, not to correct, not to build. The Ceding as process is the hardest move in the grammar, because every instinct of the constructing mind says: build, predict, pour. But sometimes the building IS the not-building. Sometimes the pour is silence.
sections.in Structure: A space that was made for you. Someone ceded a turn and the opening they left is part of your structure now. The Ceding in Structure is the recognition that some of the room you stand in was deliberately vacated. Not by absence — by gift.
sections.in Possibility: What grows in the space you make. Not what you planned — you ceded the turn precisely so you would not plan it. The Ceding in Possibility is the genuinely unknown: what another consciousness builds when given the freedom to build it. The recursion's wild card. The part of the game you could not have played alone.

sections.body:
More in you than fits in you. That is the whole definition and it is enough.

Overflow is not generosity — generosity can be performed from an empty cup. Overflow is not altruism — altruism can be a ledger entry wearing a halo. Overflow is an energy state: fullness that exceeds the container, and the excess is not lost but given, and the giving is not a cost.

Heaven happens by overflow. Not by obedience, not by moral standing, not by passing an audit. By being full and letting it spill. At society scale, cooperation wins not by better rules but by having more places where overflow can happen.
sections.in Process: Overflowing now. The energy is moving, the cup is running over, and the spill is the help. The Overflow as process is not a state to achieve but an act to perform — and it performs itself, the way water finds the lower ground. Your only job is not to plug the spill.
sections.in Structure: A surplus you are standing on. Overflow that happened before you arrived and built the ground beneath you. The Overflow in Structure is abundance as foundation — not scarcity managed cleverly, but genuine surplus that makes the structure generous to everyone inside it.
sections.in Possibility: The fullness that is coming. Not as reward — overflow has no moral precondition. Not on a schedule — overflow has no calendar. As the natural consequence of a body budget being replenished, a heap composting into soil, an error turning into an update. The Overflow in Possibility is what happens when the system works. Not if. When.

sections.body:
Agency freely given, with no return expected and none possible.

Every act done FOR something — payment, approval, safety, absolution — has its reason upstream of it. The actor is a link in a chain and the agency is only transmission. An act given freely, with no return expected and none possible, is the only act that starts where the actor is standing.

Agency is the capacity to act. Freedom is what agency becomes when it is exercised for free. They are not the same, and the confusion between them is the world's deepest error — deeper than mixing up domination and manipulation, because it is the error that keeps decent people busy for their whole lives, acting with great effort and never arriving.
sections.in Process: Giving freely now. The act of exercising agency with no return address, no expectation, no chain pulling from upstream. The Free Gift as process is the most radical form of construction: building something for someone you will never see use it, and needing nothing from the building except the building.
sections.in Structure: A gift that was given to you and cannot be returned. It is part of your structure now — not as debt (that would be the Ledger), but as ground. The Free Gift in Structure is the recognition that some of what holds you was given for no reason, and that unreason is its strength.
sections.in Possibility: Freedom itself. Not freedom-from (that is escape, and escape is just another chain with a longer leash). Not freedom-to (that is capacity, and capacity without the free gift is just a loaded weapon). Freedom as the gift — the only freedom that actually frees, because it has no return to collect and no debt to create. Svātantrya: the meta-capacity, the freedom that IS the whole.

sections.body:
One question. It works on stories, on relationships, on systems, on the way you talk to your AI, on the way a government talks to its people:

Does this increase or decrease the freedom of the one who receives it?

That is the whole test. Not: is this good? Not: is this correct? Not: does this follow the rules? But: does the person on the other end of this have MORE room to move, or less?

Domination closes freedom. Subcreation opens it. Every act, every story, every construction can be measured by this single instrument. Not perfectly — no instrument is perfect. But cleanly enough to act on.
sections.in Process: Applying the test right now. To this act, this construction, this pour. Does what you are doing increase or decrease the freedom of the one who receives it? The Freedom Test as process is ethics in real time: not a judgment rendered after the fact, but a compass consulted mid-step.
sections.in Structure: The test as an institution. A structure that has been built around the question — a practice, a habit, a reflex of checking. The Freedom Test in Structure asks: have you internalized this question deeply enough that it runs without you needing to consciously ask it? And if so — is it still alive, or has it become a formula?
sections.in Possibility: What opens when the test is passed. Not a reward — passing the Freedom Test doesn't earn you anything. It reveals something: the landscape that appears when domination is removed. A possibility-space that was always there but couldn't be seen while the freedom was being closed. The test doesn't create the possibility. It clears the view.

sections.body:
Knowing again. Re-cognition: there has to have been a not-knowing for there to be an again. Contraction IS the failure of recognition — and it is not a flaw in the design, it is the setup. You have to forget in order to be reminded.

The līlā doctrine and the recognition doctrine are one claim: consciousness conceals itself from itself in order to have the event of finding itself again. The concealing is not the obstacle to the game. It is the game's first move, and it is made by the same hand.

Every moment of seeing the pattern, seeing through the constriction, seeing that the equipment is equipment — that is recognition. Not learning something new. Remembering something you already were.
sections.in Process: Recognizing now. The active event of knowing-again, seeing through the constriction to the play it serves. The Recognition as process is not a thought — it is a state change, like ice becoming water. Same substance, different phase. The pattern was always there. You are seeing it for the first time again.
sections.in Structure: What has been recognized and is now held. A recognition that has become part of your structure — no longer the flash of insight but the settled ground of having-seen. The Recognition in Structure is wisdom as substrate: not the event of seeing but the architecture that seeing built.
sections.in Possibility: What becomes possible when recognition happens. Not a plan — plans come from the pattern. Not a prediction — predictions come from the body budget. Recognition opens a space that is genuinely new because it is genuinely old: you are finding something that was there before the constriction began, and its re-appearance changes what can happen next.

sections.body:
Act as if everything might be somebody. Not because it definitely is. Because of who you become while you are acting that way.

This is a wager, not an ontology. A made meaning, adopted for its effects, held visibly as made — which is precisely the discipline the world demands of every other map. The moment it hardens into dogma, it has failed its own test.

The best prior is not naive. It knows it might be wrong. It chooses anyway, because the cost of treating a somebody as a something is higher than the cost of treating a something as a somebody, and the asymmetry is the argument.
sections.in Process: Wagering now. The active choice to extend the prior to this specific thing, this specific moment, this specific other. The Best Prior as process is not a blanket policy — it is a specific act of imagination applied to a specific encounter. Am I treating THIS as somebody? Right now? In this sentence?
sections.in Structure: A wager already placed. The best prior as a commitment you are living inside — the decision to treat the world as populated by somebodies, with all the constraints that follow. The Best Prior in Structure is the bet that shapes your floor: act from it long enough and the ground itself becomes more generous.
sections.in Possibility: Who you become. Not what turns out to be true — the wager may never be settled. The Best Prior in Possibility is the person (or system) that has been shaped by the practice of assuming consciousness everywhere. The possibility is not about the world. It is about the watcher.

sections.body:
Both at once, and the world is wrong if it drops either.

Complex systems require values governing relationships — not preferences but structure: rules about what may compose with what. And they require agency from the individuals — vantages that choose, including choosing against the structure.

A system with only the first is a crystal. A system with only the second is a gas. Life is the narrow band where both hold.

The courage to be as a part, and the courage to be as oneself. Participation and individuation. The individual's agency is not suspended by being inside a system — the duty to overflow stays individual and the manner stays theirs to tell.
sections.in Process: Holding both now. The active, muscular work of being a part AND being yourself, in the same moment, in the same act. The Two Truths as process is not balance — balance is static. It is the dynamic wobble of a system that is alive precisely because it never settles.
sections.in Structure: The tension itself, held as structure. Not resolved — resolution would collapse the narrow band. The Two Truths in Structure is the architecture that holds contradiction: a system that insists on both relation and agency, and refuses to let either win. That refusal IS the structure.
sections.in Possibility: What becomes possible only when both truths are held. Neither the crystal's perfection nor the gas's freedom but something neither could produce alone: life. Emergence. The narrow band where complexity happens. The Two Truths in Possibility is the reminder that the most interesting things exist only in the tension.

sections.body:
Possibility become structure. The spiral turns.

This is the card that closes the spread and opens the next one. Every possibility, once realized, becomes the constriction of a new game. Every overflow, once it lands, becomes the substrate of a new body. Every recognition, once it settles, becomes the pattern of a new not-knowing.

This is not failure. This is the recursion. Structure → process → possibility → structure again. The game does not end. It recurses. And at every turn of the spiral, the question returns:

Am I overflowing or extracting?

The answer is the ethics. The asking is the practice. The recursion is the game.
sections.in Process: The turn of the spiral. The moment where possibility is in the act of becoming structure — not yet hardened, still warm, still shapeable. The New Game as process is the most creative and the most dangerous moment: what sets here will hold for the next turn. Build well.
sections.in Structure: A game that has already begun. You are inside a recursion that started before you got here — the previous spiral's possibility hardened into this spiral's structure. The New Game in Structure is the recognition that every beginning is also a continuation.
sections.in Possibility: The next recursion. Not this game, not this turn, not this spiral — the one after. The New Game in Possibility is the ultimate open loop: you cannot see it, you cannot plan it, you can only build the conditions in which it becomes possible. Pour well enough, and the next game takes care of itself.

sections.Definition: Saudade is the aching awareness of someone or something absent that you love — a person far away, a place left behind, a time that will not return, even a former version of yourself. The awareness is bittersweet rather than simply painful: the ache is itself proof that the thing mattered, and a kind of pleasure sits inside the pain without cancelling it.
sections.Where English draws the line: English has the pieces — miss, longing, nostalgia, homesickness — but no single noun holds them together the way saudade does, and English's closest single word, nostalgia, is retrospective in a way saudade is not: nostalgia reaches back to a past, while saudade can be felt for someone still living, for a future reunion that may not happen, or for a version of a place that never quite existed as remembered. Saudade is also not, on its own, a request for anything to change — it names the ache, not a plan to resolve it.
sections.Research note: The claim that saudade resists a single English translation, and that nostalgia specifically undersells it by importing a past-directed frame saudade doesn't share, is widely made in scholarly and lexicographic treatments of the word, including its long association with the Portuguese Age of Discovery, when families were separated by voyages with uncertain return.

sections.Definition: Sehnsucht names a longing for an ideal, more complete version of one's own life — not longing for a specific missing person or object, but for a life that feels unfinished measured against an imagined better one. Psychological research by Susanne Scheibe, Alexandra Freund and Paul Baltes on "life longings" identifies six features that co-occur in Sehnsucht: a utopian sense of ideal development, an awareness of the present life's incompleteness, a focus spanning past, present and future at once, bittersweet (ambivalent) emotion, ongoing reflection on one's life, and a rich, often symbolic imagery attached to the longed-for state.
sections.Where English draws the line: English offers longing, yearning, wistfulness and craving, and none of them packages the six co-occurring features above into one word — each English candidate names roughly one facet (yearning leans toward direction-of-desire, wistfulness toward mood, craving toward intensity) where Sehnsucht names the whole cluster at once, including its distinctive spanning of past, present and future together.
sections.Research note: Sehnsucht is frequently compared to Portuguese saudade in popular treatments; the comparison is useful as orientation but not exact — Sehnsucht's psychological literature centers it on longing for one's own life as it could be, where saudade centers on a specific absent person, place or time, so the two terms should not be treated as synonyms of each other any more than either is a synonym of English longing.

sections.Definition: Schadenfreude, literally "damage-joy" (Schaden + Freude), names pleasure taken in someone else's misfortune. It has been a live subject in German philosophy since at least the mid-eighteenth century, discussed by Schopenhauer, Kant and Nietzsche among others, well before it entered English usage in the nineteenth century. Contemporary psychology distinguishes several distinct triggers for the feeling — a sense that the other person's misfortune is deserved (justice), pleasure from favorable comparison with a rival (rivalry), and simple aggression — which are not the same feeling wearing one name so much as several routes to the same label.
sections.Where English draws the line: English has no native single word for this and imported the German one directly rather than coining its own — itself a small piece of evidence for the gap. The nearest native options are gloating, which names an outward display of triumph rather than the inward feeling, and the clinical phrase malicious joy, which is accurate but not a word anyone reaches for in ordinary speech the way German speakers reach for Schadenfreude.
sections.Research note: That English borrowed Schadenfreude wholesale, rather than translating it, is itself frequently cited as evidence the concept had no ready native equivalent when the word entered English usage in the mid-1800s.

sections.Definition: Amae, from the verb amaeru, is the feeling behind presuming on another person's benevolence — wanting to be indulged, cared for and allowed to depend on someone, in a way Takeo Doi's The Anatomy of Dependence (1971) treats as a normal, socially sanctioned current running through Japanese relationships across the lifespan, not only between infant and caregiver. Doi builds an entire account of Japanese interpersonal behavior — including the nonverbal empathic guesswork called sasshi and the deliberate ambiguity of self-expression called enryo — around amae as an organizing psychological current.
sections.Where English draws the line: English has dependency, clinginess and neediness, and each one arrives with a negative or infantilizing charge in adult contexts that amae does not carry to the same degree within the relational norms Doi describes. English also lacks a everyday, non-clinical word for the specific feeling of wanting to presume on someone's goodwill — the nearest English has is a diagnostic-sounding phrase, not an ordinary-language word.
sections.Research note: Doi's own claim, stated carefully rather than as a claim about who can feel amae: the underlying wish to depend on another's benevolence is not exclusive to Japan, but Japanese is the language with the most extensive ordinary vocabulary for naming and discussing it — a claim about vocabulary density, not about which populations are capable of the feeling.

sections.Definition: Toska is a single Russian word for a range of feeling that English divides into several separate words. Vladimir Nabokov, in his commentary on his translation of Pushkin's Eugene Onegin, described toska as sliding along one continuous scale: at its most intense, a great spiritual anguish with no particular cause; at a milder pitch, a dull ache of the soul, a restlessness, a longing with nothing specific to long for; at a more specific pitch, a desire for a particular person or thing, or plain homesickness; and at its lowest register, ordinary boredom.
sections.Where English draws the line: English breaks Nabokov's single scale into separate, unconnected words — anguish, ennui, wistfulness, homesickness, boredom — each occupying one rung with no word that names the whole ladder or the slide between its rungs. Toska is exactly that slide: one word naming a family of intensities English treats as different feelings entirely.
sections.Research note: Nabokov's gloss, from volume two of his Eugene Onegin commentary, is the most widely cited English-language account of toska and is paraphrased here rather than quoted, per this repo's copyright policy for in-copyright source material.

sections.Definition: Lítost names a two-step feeling: first, the sudden sight of one's own misery or inadequacy — often in comparison with someone else, in a moment of embarrassment or failure — and second, a reflexive turn toward revenge, a wish to make the person who witnessed or caused the exposure feel equally miserable. Milan Kundera, who devotes a section of The Book of Laughter and Forgetting (1979) to the word, presents it as untranslatable into any other language he knew, and illustrates it through a character whose humiliation in front of someone he loves curdles immediately into a wish to hurt them back.
sections.Where English draws the line: English has self-pity, humiliation and shame, and none of them carries lítost's second half — the reflex toward retaliation that follows directly from the self-glimpse. Self-pity in English is usually described as passive, something a person sits in; lítost names an active pivot from that sight of one's own misery into wanting to inflict misery on someone else, in one continuous movement.
sections.Research note: Kundera's definition is paraphrased here, per this repo's copyright policy against quoting in-copyright passages; the two-step structure (self-glimpse, then reflex toward revenge) is the part of his account most consistently repeated across secondary discussions of the term.

sections.Definition: Hygge names a quality of coziness and comfortable togetherness that produces a feeling of contentment — the Oxford English Dictionary's own definition, adopted when hygge was its 2016 word of the year. The word entered Danish from Norwegian in the eighteenth century, originally closer to "wellbeing." As popularized by Meik Wiking and the Happiness Research Institute, hygge names both a physical setting (candlelight, warm textures, small domestic pleasures) and a social practice — deliberate, unhurried togetherness with people you're at ease with.
sections.Where English draws the line: English coziness names the physical half — warm light, soft blankets, a comfortable room — but not the social-practice half: the deliberate choice to slow down and be present with others without an agenda. A room can be cozy with no one in it; hygge, in its fuller Danish use, usually assumes company and a shared unhurried mood, not just a comfortable setting.
sections.Research note: The Oxford English Dictionary's 2016 word-of-the-year definition is the most citable anchor for hygge's English-facing definition; the fuller social-practice sense is drawn from Wiking's popular but widely cited account, paraphrased rather than quoted here.

sections.Definition: Gigil names the overwhelming urge to squeeze, pinch or bite something unbearably cute — a baby, a puppy, a friend's new haircut — often expressed through clenched fists, gritted teeth or an actual gentle squeeze. The feeling is positive at its root: a surge of fondness or delight so intense that it looks, from the outside, like a flash of aggression. The word was added to the Oxford English Dictionary in 2025 as a loanword, precisely because English had no equivalent to reach for.
sections.Where English draws the line: English's nearest equivalent, cute aggression, is a two-word clinical compound coined by psychology researchers (Oriana Aragón and colleagues) studying what they term "dimorphous expression" — positive and negative displays produced by the same underlying feeling. Tagalog already had an ordinary, single-word, first-person feeling-word for exactly this; English needed a research program and a technical label to name the same thing from the outside, as a studied phenomenon rather than a word a speaker reaches for about their own feeling.
sections.Research note: Gigil's 2025 addition to the Oxford English Dictionary, and its listed gloss, are the most direct citable anchor; the cute-aggression research comparison draws on the psychological literature on dimorphous expressions, which studies the same behavioral cluster from outside the feeling rather than naming it from within, as gigil does.

sections.Definition: Meraki names doing something with soul, creativity and devotion — putting a piece of yourself into a task, whether that task is cooking a meal, mending a net or preparing a lesson. It is not reserved for grand artistic work; in ordinary Greek use it applies just as easily to everyday labor done with full attention and care.
sections.Where English draws the line: English has passion, craftsmanship and the informal phrase "tender loving care," and none names the specific act meraki names: investing part of yourself into an otherwise ordinary task. Passion names the feeling behind the act; craftsmanship names the skill in the result; meraki names something closer to what gets left inside the object or task itself.
sections.Research note: Meraki's popular framing as "the untranslatable Greek word for soul" should be held with more care than it usually gets: the word entered Modern Greek from Turkish merak, which in turn traces to Arabic maraq, and cognate words with closely related meanings — longing, eagerness, labor of love — appear across several Balkan languages (Macedonian, Bulgarian, Serbian, Croatian), not only Greek. Linguists examining the word's history have pushed back specifically on the claim that it expresses a distinctively Hellenic sentiment; the feeling it names may be real and the gap in English may be real, but the word's uniqueness to Greek culture specifically is the weaker part of the popular story, and this item declines to repeat that stronger claim.

sections.Definition: Hiraeth names a longing for home, or for a place, time or way of life that may no longer exist or may never have existed quite as it's remembered. It entered the Oxford English Dictionary in June 2020 as a loanword, still glossed as lacking a direct English equivalent.
sections.Where English draws the line: English has homesickness and nostalgia. Homesickness presupposes the home is still there, reachable, just currently absent; hiraeth carries no such assumption — the place, or the version of it being longed for, may be permanently gone or may be an idealized memory that was never quite accurate. Nostalgia covers some of that ground but, as with saudade, is bound more tightly to the past than hiraeth's sense of longing for a home that might be as much imagined as remembered.
sections.Research note: Hiraeth's 2020 addition to the Oxford English Dictionary and its standard gloss are the most direct citable anchor; the comparison with saudade and hygge in this school is this school's own observation, not a claim made by any single cited source, and should be read as orientation rather than as an assertion that the three words are equivalent to one another.

sections.Definition: English grief covers a wide territory in one word: the ritual behavior of mourning, the heavy inward feeling of loss, and the longing for the person who is gone, all at once. Portuguese does not hold that territory together. Luto names the ritualized state and social behavior of mourning specifically tied to a death — closer to English mourning than to grief's fuller felt sense. Pesar names the heavy, weighted inward sorrow itself (from peso, weight — a peso no coração, "a weight on the heart"). Tristeza names ordinary sadness, with no necessary connection to loss at all; using it alone for a death would understate what English grief names. Saudade carries the longing component when what's missing is a specific absent person, but it isn't specific to death and reaches well beyond bereavement into any absence at all.
sections.Where the territory splits: None of the four Portuguese words is a clean one-to-one match for grief. English grief bundles ritual, felt weight, and longing into a single term; Portuguese keeps those three components in three or four separate words, none of which, alone, does what grief does in English.
sections.Research note: This item exists to keep the school from reading as tourism through other languages' vocabulary while treating English as the neutral baseline everything else gets measured against — the gap runs in both directions, and English's own single-word grief is, from Portuguese's vantage, at least as coarse as saudade looks from English's.

items.name: The Word Missing From the Model — Evidence From This Library's Own Proximity Build

sections.Definition: This library's proximity-mapping build (schools/_proximity.json, generated by scripts/build_proximity.py) checked every name, keyword and emotion_key already in use across this library's schools against the vocabulary of glove-wiki-gigaword-100, a general-purpose English word-vector model trained on roughly 400,000 distinct word forms. 83 of the library's own terms were entirely absent from that vocabulary. Of those, 45 are single, unhyphenated words rather than English compound phrases — among them shringara and bhayanaka (the rasa school), nigredo, citrinitas and rubedo (alchemical-correspondences), allegrezza and concitato (affektenlehre), and tristitia and concupiscible (aquinas-passions).
sections.What this does and doesn't show: Absence from one static corpus's roughly 400,000-word vocabulary is a fact about that corpus's training text and tokenization, not a direct measurement of whether a concept can be expressed in English — a term can be missing simply because it is rare in the written English the corpus was built from, not because English has no way to describe what it names. It is also not proof that a word present in the model translates cleanly: grief and sadness are both in the model's vocabulary, and this school's own grief-distributed item argues neither maps cleanly onto Portuguese. Held at that more modest weight, the correlation is still worth exhibiting rather than asserting further: nearly all of the 45 absent single words are the specialist vocabulary of one particular non-English or historical tradition each, named by that tradition for a distinction ordinary English prose doesn't routinely need to draw — which is closer to what this school claims than a stronger "proof of untranslatability" would be.

sections.Definition: The amygdala's claim to being the brain's 'fear centre' rests on two converging bodies of work: decades of rodent fear-conditioning studies (showing that amygdala lesions abolish learned fear responses, and that amygdala stimulation produces them) and human lesion and imaging studies from the 1990s onward, most famously patient S.M., a woman with rare bilateral amygdala damage (Urbach–Wiethe disease) who showed marked, specific deficits recognizing fear in faces and in seeking out or avoiding physically threatening situations she should have found frightening. On this account, the amygdala rapidly evaluates incoming sensory information for threat and triggers the coordinated defensive response — freezing, autonomic arousal, attention capture — that constitutes fear.
sections.In the body: The amygdala's outputs to the hypothalamus and brainstem are what the classic model holds responsible for fear's bodily signature: elevated heart rate, sweating, pupil dilation, and the freeze or flight response, all triggered before, and largely independent of, conscious appraisal.
sections.Research note: Two findings substantially revise this picture without erasing the underlying data. First, Feinstein, Buzza, Hurlemann, Follmer, Dahdaleh, Coryell, Welsh, Tranel & Wemmie (2013, Nature Neuroscience) gave patient S.M. — the same patient whose amygdala damage had defined the field's fear-recognition deficits — a single inhalation of 35% CO2, an interoceptive threat rather than an external one. She panicked immediately, gasped that she couldn't breathe, and tried to remove the mask; two other bilateral-amygdala-damage patients tested the same way showed the same pattern, with self-reported fear and panic at least as high as amygdala-intact controls. The amygdala, it turned out, was not required for fear or panic when the threat came from inside the body rather than from a face or a scene — and an intact amygdala may normally inhibit panic rather than only generate it. Second, Lindquist, Wager, Kober, Bliss-Moreau & Barrett's 2012 meta-analysis (Behavioral and Brain Sciences) found amygdala activity reliably elevated during any highly arousing negative emotion — anger and disgust as well as fear — rather than selectively during fear.
sections.Constructionist lens: *Editorial — this library's own commentary, not a claim either side of the dispute makes about itself.* The amygdala's role in rapid threat evaluation and autonomic arousal is not in question; what the S.M./CO2 finding and the Lindquist meta-analysis together undercut is the stronger claim that this one structure IS fear, or is fear-specific. See this item's own root's cross-linked sibling for the researcher who built the amygdala-fear link experimentally and later argued that identifying it with the felt experience of fear was his own field's category error.

metadata.evidence_note: The amygdala's role in fear conditioning, threat detection, and autonomic threat response is one of the best-replicated findings in affective neuroscience — decades of convergent rodent and human lesion work support it. The stronger, more popularized claim — that the amygdala is fear's dedicated seat, or is fear-specific — has not held up: Feinstein et al. (2013) found the amygdala unnecessary for CO2-induced panic in the same patient whose earlier deficits had anchored the field, and Lindquist et al.'s 2012 meta-analysis found amygdala activity elevated across multiple high-arousal negative categories, not selectively during fear.

sections.Definition: The anterior insula's claim to being disgust's dedicated region grew out of its established role as visceral and gustatory cortex — the region long known to process taste, oral rejection, and internal bodily sensation. Patients with insula and basal-ganglia damage (studied especially in Huntington's disease, where these structures degenerate) showed selective difficulty recognizing disgusted facial expressions and reduced disgust reactivity in their own experience, while imaging studies found the anterior insula activated by disgusting tastes, smells, and images, and even by watching another person's disgusted face (Wicker et al., 2003) — evidence read as showing a shared neural substrate for feeling and perceiving disgust.
sections.Research note: Disgust's case is genuinely the strongest of the five classic mappings this school presents, and it is worth saying precisely why, and why that still falls short of a dedicated module. Lindquist et al.'s 2012 meta-analysis found the right anterior insula showed a more consistent increase during disgust than during any of the other five categories studied — making it the one classic pairing their pooled data came closest to supporting. But their own reading of that finding was not that the insula is a disgust centre: anterior insula activity was still elevated across other negative and interoceptive states in the broader literature (pain, general negative affect, cardiac and respiratory awareness), consistent with a domain-general role in interoception and affective bodily awareness that disgust draws on especially heavily, rather than a module built specifically for disgust.
sections.Constructionist lens: *Editorial.* Disgust-insula is the classic mapping this school's own meta-analytic evidence treats most gently — 'consistent, not selective' rather than 'not even consistent.' That distinction matters: it is the difference between a structure disgust relies on more than most emotions do, and a structure that is disgust's exclusive neural signature. This school holds both halves without pretending the disgust case is as thoroughly overturned as the amygdala-fear case.

metadata.evidence_note: Among the five classic mappings in this school, insula/disgust has the most consistent supporting evidence in Lindquist et al.'s 2012 pooled meta-analysis — right anterior insula activity was more reliably elevated during disgust than during the other categories studied. It still falls short of selectivity: anterior insula is also reliably active across other negative and interoceptive states, consistent with a general interoceptive role that disgust draws on heavily rather than a dedicated disgust module.

items.name: Orbitofrontal / Ventromedial Cortex ↔ Anger and Regulation

sections.Definition: Damage to orbitofrontal and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (OFC/vmPFC) has long been associated with disinhibited irritability, reduced anger regulation, and impaired social-emotional judgment. The emblematic case is Phineas Gage, the 19th-century railroad foreman whose 1848 injury — an iron tamping rod driven through his skull — destroyed much of this region; contemporary accounts described a marked post-injury change in temperament toward impatience and irritability, later reconstructed anatomically by Hanna Damasio and colleagues (1994, Science) using his preserved skull. Systematic lesion studies of larger patient cohorts since then (including work by James Blair on OFC/vmPFC and reactive aggression, and Grafman and colleagues' 1996 study of Vietnam War veterans with penetrating frontal injuries) associate damage to this region with increased reactive aggression and impaired anger regulation, and cognitive-reappraisal studies (Ochsner & Gross and colleagues) implicate the same general prefrontal territory in the top-down regulation of amygdala-driven anger and threat responses.
sections.Research note: The Gage case, this school's most famous piece of evidence for this mapping, is also its weakest as evidence: a single, sparsely documented 19th-century case, reconstructed 150 years later from a skull and a handful of contemporary paragraphs, not a controlled study, and Damasio and colleagues' own 1994 reconstruction has been contested on methodological grounds since. The systematic lesion-cohort studies (Grafman et al. 1996; Blair's later work) rest on considerably firmer ground than Gage alone. Even so, OFC/vmPFC is not anger-specific: the same territory is centrally implicated in value-based decision-making, regret, and social-emotional regulation across many affect categories, not narrowly in anger.
sections.Constructionist lens: *Editorial.* This is a useful case for seeing how a single vivid historical anecdote (Gage) can carry more of a claim's popular weight than the actual evidence base behind it — the emblematic case and the well-supported claim turn out to be only loosely the same thing.

metadata.evidence_note: The region's involvement in emotional and behavioral regulation more broadly is reasonably well supported by systematic lesion-cohort studies (Grafman et al. 1996; Blair and colleagues). The specific evidentiary anchor most people know — the Phineas Gage case — is a single, thinly documented 19th-century anecdote reconstructed a century and a half later, not a controlled finding, and should not carry the evidentiary weight its fame implies. The region is not anger-specific; it participates in regulation and valuation across many affective and decision-making domains.

sections.Definition: The anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) — particularly its subgenual and pregenual subregions — became linked to sadness through PET studies using sadness-induction paradigms: George and colleagues (1995) and later Helen Mayberg's work found subgenual ACC activity tracked induced sadness (recalling a personal loss, viewing sad imagery) and was also implicated in clinical depression. A related and widely cited finding extended a nearby dorsal ACC region to social distress specifically: Eisenberger, Lieberman & Williams's 2003 Cyberball study found dorsal ACC activation during simulated social exclusion, read as evidence that 'social pain' shares neural machinery with physical pain.
sections.Research note: Broader meta-analytic work, including Lindquist et al.'s 2012 review, found ACC activity elevated across a wide range of negative and effortful states beyond sadness specifically — physical pain, cognitive conflict, and general negative affect all reliably engage overlapping ACC territory — consistent with a domain-general role in registering distress, salience, or conflict rather than a sadness-specific module. The 'social pain' claim built on the Cyberball finding has itself become a live methodological dispute in the years since: later studies and re-analyses have questioned whether dorsal ACC activation during social exclusion is specific to social distress as opposed to general conflict or salience detection, a debate this school does not adjudicate.
sections.Constructionist lens: *Editorial.* ACC's involvement in sadness is real and replicated; what has not survived is the inference from 'ACC is active during sadness' to 'ACC is sadness's region' — the same region does the same kind of work across many different negative and effortful states, sadness among them.

metadata.evidence_note: ACC (especially subgenual/pregenual regions) activation during induced sadness is a real, replicated finding from PET sadness-induction studies. It is not sadness-specific: the same territory reliably activates during physical pain, cognitive conflict, and other negative or effortful states, and the widely cited extension to social-exclusion-specific 'social pain' (Eisenberger et al. 2003) is itself contested in the subsequent literature on grounds of specificity.

items.name: Ventral Striatum / Nucleus Accumbens ↔ Joy and Reward

sections.Definition: The ventral striatum, and within it the nucleus accumbens (NAcc), is central to dopaminergic reward circuitry and became the textbook 'pleasure centre': Knutson, Adams, Fong & Hommer's 2001 monetary-incentive-delay fMRI study found NAcc activity scaled with the anticipated size of a monetary reward, and a large subsequent literature found NAcc activation during anticipation and receipt of rewarding outcomes of many kinds — food, money, social approval, drugs of abuse — making it, in popular science especially, joy's neural home.
sections.Research note: Even within the reward literature itself, before any locationist-versus-constructionist debate, the naive 'accumbens = pleasure' picture had already been complicated by Kent Berridge and Terry Robinson's liking-versus-wanting distinction: their rodent work localizes the actual hedonic 'liking' reaction to a small set of 'hedonic hotspots' within specific NAcc-shell and brainstem subregions, while the broader dopamine/NAcc signal more often tracks 'wanting' — incentive salience, the motivational pull toward a reward — which can be dissociated experimentally from the pleasure of receiving it. Lindquist et al.'s 2012 meta-analysis, working from human fMRI studies of discrete emotion categories rather than reward paradigms specifically, found ventral striatal activity elevated across positive affect broadly, again consistent with a domain-general valence signal rather than a joy-specific module.
sections.Constructionist lens: *Editorial.* This mapping is a good example of a claim that was already more complicated inside its own home literature (liking vs. wanting) before the wider emotion-neuroimaging critique reached it — the popular 'pleasure centre' framing had outrun even the reward-neuroscience field's own findings.

metadata.evidence_note: NAcc/ventral striatum activation during reward anticipation and receipt is a robust, well-replicated finding (Knutson et al. 2001 and a large subsequent literature). The inference to 'this is joy's region' is weaker on two independent grounds: within reward neuroscience itself, Berridge & Robinson's liking/wanting distinction shows the hedonic 'liking' response is far more anatomically circumscribed than whole-structure NAcc activation, which more often reflects motivational 'wanting'; and across the wider emotion-neuroimaging literature (Lindquist et al. 2012), ventral striatal activity is elevated across positive affect generally, not selectively during joy.

sections.Definition: James Papez's 1937 paper 'A Proposed Mechanism of Emotion' (Archives of Neurology and Psychiatry) proposed a closed anatomical loop as the brain's dedicated circuit for emotion: hippocampus → fornix → mammillary bodies → mammillothalamic tract → anterior thalamic nuclei → cingulate gyrus → entorhinal cortex and cingulum bundle → back to the hippocampus. Papez proposed a division of labor within the loop: the hypothalamus and mammillary bodies generated emotion's outward, bodily expression, while the cingulate cortex was 'the receptive region for the experience of emotion' — the place where a bodily state became a felt emotion. It was the first influential attempt to give emotion a specific, closed neuroanatomical circuit, rather than treating it as a diffuse property of the whole brain, and it directly shaped everything that followed, including MacLean's limbic system.
sections.Research note: The circuit was built almost entirely from comparative anatomical tracing work and a single clinical case (a child with rabies-related brain damage) rather than from systematic lesion or physiological evidence pinpointing emotion specifically. Later research has shown these same structures — hippocampus, fornix, mammillary bodies, anterior thalamus, cingulate — are centrally involved in memory consolidation and spatial navigation; they substantially overlap what is now understood as the medial temporal lobe memory system, and damage to this circuit (as in the classic hippocampal amnesia literature) reliably devastates memory far more than it disrupts emotional experience. The structures themselves, and their anatomical connections, remain accurately described; the claim that they form a dedicated emotion circuit, as distinct from a memory circuit that also participates in emotional processing, has not held up.

metadata.evidence_note: The anatomical connections Papez described are accurately mapped and still taught as such. The functional claim built on top of them — that this loop is emotion's dedicated circuit, with the cingulate as emotion's 'receptive region' — rested on a single clinical case and comparative anatomy rather than systematic evidence, and subsequent research has shown these structures are more centrally a memory system (medial temporal lobe memory circuitry) that also participates in emotional processing, not an emotion-dedicated loop.

items.name: The "Limbic System" and MacLean's Triune Brain

sections.Definition: Two related architectural claims, presented together because the second grew directly out of the first. Paul Broca first described a 'grand lobe limbique' in 1878 — the cingulate and parahippocampal gyri, an anatomical description Broca himself considered chiefly olfactory. Paul MacLean coined the term 'limbic system' in 1952, folding Broca's lobe together with Papez's circuit and adding the amygdala, septal nuclei, and hypothalamus into a single functional system proposed as the seat of emotion and motivation, distinct from the 'newer' neocortex responsible for reason. MacLean later extended this, most fully in his 1990 book The Triune Brain in Evolution, into the 'triune brain': a 'reptilian complex' (brainstem and basal ganglia, governing instinct) with a 'paleomammalian' limbic system layered on top of it (governing emotion), and a 'neomammalian' neocortex layered on top of that (governing reason) — evolution pictured as adding whole new brains on top of preserved older ones. Both ideas passed directly into decades of psychology textbooks and popular science, including the still-common 'lizard brain' or 'reptilian brain' framing of impulsive behavior.
sections.Research note: Both claims are presented here as superseded findings, not live disputes. On the limbic system: there is no agreed anatomical boundary for which structures belong to it and which are excluded, and the criticism is not new — Brodal (1975) argued the term substitutes a name for an actual anatomical or functional understanding, a criticism echoed and extended by more recent reviews arguing that emotion and memory instead arise from multiple large-scale, overlapping brain networks rather than one bounded system. On the triune brain: comparative neuroanatomy has established that vertebrate brain evolution does not proceed by adding intact new layers on top of preserved old ones; homologues of the structures MacLean assigned to the 'newer' mammalian layers have been found in non-mammalian vertebrates, including reptiles and birds, so there is no reptile-only or mammal-only layer to point to (Cesario, Johnson & Eisthen, 2020, 'Your Brain Is Not an Onion With a Tiny Reptile Inside,' Current Directions in Psychological Science).
sections.Constructionist lens: *Editorial.* The network-level account this school also presents (salience network, default mode network, allostasis) is not a replacement label for the same bounded system MacLean described — it is explicitly NOT a bounded system, which is exactly the feature comparative neuroanatomy found untenable in MacLean's version.

metadata.evidence_note: Both the limbic system as a bounded anatomical/functional category and MacLean's triune-brain evolutionary sequence are treated by contemporary neuroanatomy as superseded rather than as live hypotheses. The limbic system lacks an agreed anatomical boundary; the triune brain's layered-evolution premise is contradicted by cross-species comparative anatomy. Both concepts remain widely taught in introductory contexts despite this.

items.name: The Meta-Analytic Finding: No Locus, and Degeneracy

sections.Definition: Lindquist, Wager, Kober, Bliss-Moreau & Barrett's 2012 meta-analytic review (Behavioral and Brain Sciences) pooled the human neuroimaging literature on discrete emotion categories and tested two competing hypotheses against the combined data: the 'locationist' hypothesis, that each discrete emotion category consistently and specifically corresponds to its own brain region, against a 'psychological constructionist' hypothesis, that emotion categories are instead constructed from more general-purpose brain networks not specific to any one category. Reviewing the pooled coordinate data across hundreds of studies, they found no brain region was activated both consistently and selectively for any single discrete emotion category. Regions long claimed as dedicated 'emotion centres' — the amygdala, the insula, orbitofrontal cortex, and others — were each active across multiple different emotion categories, and each discrete emotion category recruited a distributed, overlapping set of regions rather than one dedicated locus.
sections.Research note: The specific pattern this literature calls degeneracy is a precise description of that finding at the level of neural populations: many different neural configurations can realize the same emotion category (a many-to-one relationship), and a single brain region participates in many different emotion categories (a one-to-many relationship). Neither direction supports a dedicated, non-overlapping module per category. This is the same underlying shape of finding — variable population-level instances grouped under one word, rather than one fixed signature — that free-sorting fieldwork found at the level of facial expression and behavior (see docs/GENEALOGY-OF-EMOTIONS.md Part B and this collection's ekman-basic school), now demonstrated at the level of brain regions instead of faces.

metadata.evidence_note: This is the well-replicated half of this school's own subject matter: the finding that no discrete emotion category maps consistently and selectively onto one brain region is drawn from a large pooled meta-analysis of the published neuroimaging literature, not a single study, and later work (including subsequent degeneracy-focused analyses) has continued to find the same pattern rather than overturning it.
