sections.Definition: Patākā ("flag") is the first hasta taught to a beginning student and the simplest in construction: the palm faces forward or downward, all four fingers extended straight and held close together, and the thumb bent in toward the base of the index finger. Nothing is curled, crossed, or spread — it is the flat, open hand.
sections.Viniyoga — what it may signify: The Abhinaya Darpaṇa's own viniyoga verse for patākā runs to several dozen entries, easily the longest of any single hasta. A representative selection: clouds, forests, night, a river or the ocean, wind, moonlight and strong sunlight, torrential rain, a shower of flowers, taking an oath, prohibition and the word "stop," a blessing, protection, covering or density, a crowd, height, a door being forced open or closed, a shield, and the numeral one. The same flat hand, in other words, stands for weather, for a body of water, for a moral act (an oath), and for a spoken refusal — resolved only by what the performance is doing at that moment.
sections.Research note: Patākā's viniyoga list is the clearest single illustration of this school's central claim: one shape, dozens of unrelated meanings, disambiguated entirely by context rather than by the hand itself.

sections.Definition: Tripatākā ("three-part flag") starts from patākā and bends only the ring finger down toward the palm, leaving the index, middle, and little fingers, plus the thumb, extended.
sections.Viniyoga — what it may signify: Used alone, tripatākā's viniyoga includes invocation, descent, bidding farewell, prohibition, entrance, raising an object, bowing or salutation, touching the head with an auspicious object, putting on a crown or turban, wiping away tears, drawing a tilaka mark, and the flight of small birds. In the Abhinaya Darpaṇa it is also given specifically as a crown, a tree, the thunderbolt weapon (vajra) and its wielder Indra, a lamp or rising flame, and a pigeon. Used two-handed, its viniyoga shifts further — adoration of feet, marriage, a king, planets, ascetics, doors, sea monsters, and a king's procession.
sections.Research note: Tripatākā shows the other half of this school's claim: the same crown, tree, and blessing meanings that could in principle be carried by other hastas are, by convention, carried by this one — a meaning finding its gesture rather than a gesture fixing its meaning.

sections.Definition: Ardhacandra ("half moon") begins from patākā and draws the thumb outward and away from the index finger, opening a curved gap between them that echoes the shape of a crescent moon.
sections.Viniyoga — what it may signify: Its viniyoga includes a young sapling, the crescent moon itself, a conch shell, a water jar, a bracelet, forcing something open, exertion, drinking, the moon's eighth-day phase, seizing a throat, a spear, consecrating an image, a platter, an origin, meditation or musing, and greeting an ordinary person. For a female character specifically it can also signify a girdle, the hip, the waist, the face, or an ear ornament.
sections.Research note: The crescent-moon meaning here sits alongside a full-moon meaning carried by a different hasta, alapadma, in this same school — one referent, the moon, distributed across two unrelated hand shapes depending on which phase of it is meant.

sections.Definition: Śikhara ("peak" or "spire") begins from muṣṭi, a closed fist, and raises the thumb straight upward while the remaining four fingers stay curled into the palm.
sections.Viniyoga — what it may signify: Its viniyoga includes reins, a whip or goad, a bow, a javelin, painting the lips or feet, arranging hair, Manmatha (the god of desire), a pillar, certainty, making an offering to ancestors, the upper lip, entering a place, teeth, a question, saying "no," an intimate suggestion, an embrace, and the ringing of a bell.
sections.Research note: Śikhara's pairing with Manmatha, the god of desire, and with an embrace sits directly inside the same semantic territory schools/rasa's śṛṅgāra item covers — a hasta doing, in gesture, part of the work rasa theory analyzes at the level of a whole performance.

sections.Definition: Kartarīmukha ("scissors-face") begins from ardhapatākā, joins the tips of the thumb, ring finger, and little finger, and separates the index and middle fingers so they open and close like the two blades of a pair of scissors.
sections.Viniyoga — what it may signify: Held with fingers down, it can show the way, or a baby crawling. Held with fingers up, it can show biting, horns, or the act of writing letters. Other positions of the same hand give falling, death, transgression, reversal, and putting something into another's trust; combined with another hand or alone it can show an antelope, a yak, a buffalo, a temple elephant, a bull, a gate, or a hilltop. The Abhinaya Darpaṇa also gives it for the separation of a man and woman, opposition, plundering, the corner of an eye, estrangement, lightning, sleeping alone, and weeping.
sections.Research note: Few hastas in this set carry a wider spread of viniyoga than kartarīmukha — animal horns, a lover's estrangement, and lightning share one shape, which is exactly the resolved-by-context structure this school states as its argument.

sections.Definition: Kaṭakāmukha ("link-in-a-bangle mouth") begins from kapittha and brings the tip of the index finger to touch the tips of the thumb and middle finger, while the ring and little fingers lift and bend slightly away.
sections.Viniyoga — what it may signify: Its viniyoga includes plucking a flower, stringing a garland or a pearl necklace, drawing an arrow to the string of a bow, offering a betel leaf, preparing a fragrant paste, smelling, speaking, and glancing. It is also given for sacrifice or oblation, an umbrella, gathering reins, a fan, holding a mirror, drawing a decorative pattern, applying powder, wielding a long stick or whip, drawing out a goad or rope, and representing a woman in general.
sections.Research note: Kaṭakāmukha is the twelfth of the 28 asaṃyuta hastas in the Abhinaya Darpaṇa's own sequence; several of its meanings (garland-stringing, offering betel, applying fragrant paste) belong to the same courtship and adornment register śikhara and ardhacandra also touch, from a differently shaped hand.

sections.Definition: Alapadma ("unfolded lotus") spreads all five fingers apart and curves each slightly backward from its base — the little finger bent the most, the index the least — with the thumb drawn slightly outward, so the whole hand opens like a lotus in full bloom.
sections.Viniyoga — what it may signify: Its viniyoga includes a fully blossomed lotus, an elephant-apple, a circular or turning movement, beauty, longing for a beloved, a woman's own self-reference (including, in some readings, the breast), a mirror, a hair-knot, the full moon, a moon-pavilion or turret, a village, height, anger, a lake, the Chakravaka bird, a murmuring sound, and praise. Used alone it can also mark negation — "it is not," "nonsense."
sections.Research note: Alapadma's "longing for a beloved" and full-moon meanings sit close to schools/rasa's śṛṅgāra (built from rati, romantic longing) — see the cross-link on this item. The same emotional territory a whole performance builds toward in rasa theory is, in āngika abhinaya, also carried moment to moment by a single hand shape.

sections.Definition: Añjali is a saṃyuta (joined-hand) hasta: two patākā hands are brought together, palm to palm, fingers aligned and touching along their full length. Where every other item in this school is a single-hand shape, añjali is included because it is the one saṃyuta hasta almost everyone outside the dance tradition already recognizes — the gesture that survives into everyday Indian greeting as namaste.
sections.Viniyoga — what it may signify: The Abhinaya Darpaṇa gives añjali a single, tightly specified use — salutation — but makes the meaning depend on where the joined hands are held: above the head for a deity, in front of the face for a teacher, and in front of the chest for a learned person (a Brahmin, in the text's own terms). One shape, one broad meaning (reverence), but the meaning's precise addressee is set by height alone — a different axis of context-dependence from patākā's many unrelated meanings in one fixed position.
sections.Research note: Añjali is the sole saṃyuta hasta itemized in this skeleton; the Abhinaya Darpaṇa names 23 more, several (kapota, karkaṭa, svastika, puṣpapuṭa) with their own multi-item viniyoga lists left for a future pass.

sections.Definition: In Rhetoric II.2, Aristotle defines anger (orgē) as a desire, accompanied by pain, for conspicuous revenge for a conspicuous and unjustified slight directed at oneself or someone close to one. It is not raw physiological arousal; it is an appraisal — a judgment that one has been wronged and belittled — paired with the expectation that retaliation will be pleasant.
sections.Rhetoric-bound, not clinical: Aristotle is not describing anger as a state to be diagnosed or managed. He is telling an orator which beliefs make an audience angry — being slighted by people who owe them respect — so a speech can provoke that anger against an opponent, or calm it (praotēs, the paired state) in a judge who has been roused against the speaker's own client.
sections.Research note: Aristotle treats anger as an object-directed judgment rather than a mood — a cognitive-appraisal reading of emotion that anticipates, without duplicating, both Stoic theory and modern appraisal theories such as Richard Lazarus's (1991).

sections.Definition: Rhetoric II.8 defines pity (eleos) as pain at an apparently destructive or painful event happening to someone who does not deserve it, which the observer might expect could happen to himself or someone close to him. Both conditions matter: the suffering must look undeserved, and the observer must see it as possible for themselves — Aristotle notes that people who feel invulnerable feel less pity.
sections.Rhetoric-bound, not clinical: Pity here is a lever, not a syndrome. Aristotle catalogues what makes a courtroom audience pity a defendant — visible, specific, nearby suffering, a person like the listener — because a speaker who understands the lever can pull it.
sections.Research note: Aristotle explicitly pairs eleos with nemesis (indignation at another's undeserved good fortune) as mirror-image judgments about desert, not as unrelated feelings — a structural pairing this skeleton does not yet include as its own item.

sections.Definition: Rhetoric II.3 defines growing calm (praotēs) as a settling or quieting of anger, its direct contrary. People grow calm toward those who admit fault and show grief at what they have done, toward those who humble themselves and offer no resistance, and toward those who acted involuntarily — in each case the belief that one has been deliberately wronged and belittled, which orgē requires, is undone.
sections.Rhetoric-bound, not clinical: Aristotle presents praotēs as a lever just like orgē's own — an orator defending a client wants to know exactly which admissions or postures will cool a judge's anger, not to describe calm as a virtue in its own right (that discussion belongs to the Nicomachean Ethics, not the Rhetoric).
sections.Research note: The orgē/praotēs pair is the first of fourteen pathē catalogued across Rhetoric II.2–11 and sets the pattern the rest follow: each pathos is defined by the belief that produces it, the person it targets, and the belief that cancels it out again.

sections.Definition: Rhetoric II.4 defines philia (friendly feeling) as wishing for someone what one believes to be good, for that person's own sake rather than one's own, and being inclined to bring it about so far as one is able. Philoi (friends) are those who feel this toward each other and know that they do.
sections.Rhetoric-bound, not clinical: Unlike the Nicomachean Ethics's extended treatment of philia as a form of virtuous relationship, the Rhetoric's interest is narrower: which beliefs make an audience feel friendly disposed toward a speaker or a defendant, so a speech can cultivate or exploit that disposition.
sections.Research note: Aristotle pairs philia with its contrary, echthra (enmity/hatred), in the same chapter — not included as its own item in this skeleton — and the pairing anticipates a structural feature of nearly every pathos in Book II: each is defined partly by naming the state that cancels it.

sections.Definition: Rhetoric II.5 defines fear (phobos) as pain or disturbance from the appearance of an imminent evil that is destructive or painful — specifically, an evil that appears near at hand rather than remote, and within someone's power to inflict.
sections.Rhetoric-bound, not clinical: Aristotle catalogues exactly what makes danger seem near rather than far — signs of hostile intent, evidence of ability to harm, precedent of similar people suffering similar harm — because a speaker who wants a jury frightened of an outcome needs to make it feel close, not just possible.
sections.Research note: Aristotle pairs phobos with tharsos (confidence, below) as direct contraries sharing one object — an apprehended danger — and differing only in how near or resistible it appears. The Stoic phobos above shares this item's emotion_key but is a different project: an ethical claim about a false judgment, not a rhetorical appraisal of nearness.

metadata.deck: Greek Pathē — Rhetoric and Stoic Ethics

sections.Definition: Rhetoric II.5 defines confidence (tharsos) as the direct contrary of fear: an expectation of safety, felt when what is dangerous seems either non-existent, far off, or well within one's power to resist — the hopeful counterpart to fear's felt nearness of harm.
sections.Rhetoric-bound, not clinical: Paired with phobos in the same chapter, tharsos gives the orator the flip side of the same lever — showing an audience that a danger is remote, resistible, or already overcome by people like them removes fear and installs confidence in its place.
sections.Research note: Aristotle notes people feel tharsos when they believe they have often escaped or overcome danger before, and when they see allies, resources, or means of safety available to them — a proto-appraisal account of confidence as a judgment about one's own resources relative to the threat.

metadata.deck: Greek Pathē — Rhetoric and Stoic Ethics

sections.Definition: Rhetoric II.6 defines shame (aischynē) as a pain or disturbance concerning present, past, or future faults that appear likely to bring one into disrepute — felt specifically before people whose opinion one values: those close to us, those we admire, or those who will judge us.
sections.Rhetoric-bound, not clinical: Aristotle's interest is in which disgraceful acts a speaker can make an audience feel, or fear feeling, ashamed of — cowardice, injustice, self-indulgence — and before whom that shame lands hardest, since shame felt before a stranger one will never see again barely registers by comparison.
sections.Research note: Aristotle pairs aischynē with anaischyntia (shamelessness) as its contrary in the same chapter, and ties shame closely to a concern for reputation rather than to private conscience alone — a social, audience-facing reading consistent with the Rhetoric's overall approach.

sections.Definition: Rhetoric II.7 defines kindness (charis) as helpfulness shown to someone in need, given not in return for anything and not for the helper's own advantage but for the sake of the person helped — greater the more urgent, important, or difficult-to-obtain the need, and greater still if the helper acted alone or first.
sections.Rhetoric-bound, not clinical: This chapter tells a speaker how to make a past favor look as large as possible — or, arguing the other side, how to make a claimed favor look smaller, self-interested, or trivial — rather than analyzing gratitude as a virtue.
sections.Research note: Charis is one of the few pathē in this part of the Rhetoric defined primarily by an action performed (helping) rather than by a belief about one's own situation — its emotional charge lies in how the recipient and observers interpret the giver's motive.

sections.Definition: Rhetoric II.9 defines nemesis (righteous indignation) as pain at the sight of undeserved good fortune — the structural mirror of eleos (pity, above): both are judgments about desert, one triggered by undeserved suffering, the other by undeserved success.
sections.Rhetoric-bound, not clinical: Aristotle tells a speaker exactly which strokes of fortune provoke indignation in a listener — sudden wealth, power, or honor landing on someone judged to lack the virtue that ought to earn it — so an opponent's undeserved advantage can be made to sting rather than simply impress.
sections.Research note: Aristotle explicitly pairs nemesis with eleos as mirror-image judgments about desert, and separately treats nemesis in the Nicomachean Ethics as a mean state, felt rightly only toward genuinely undeserved fortune — its excess, feeling pain even at deserved good fortune, is phthonos (envy, next).

metadata.deck: Greek Pathē — Rhetoric and Stoic Ethics

sections.Definition: Rhetoric II.10 defines envy (phthonos) as pain at the good fortune of people like oneself — equals in birth, ability, possessions, or reputation — not because their good fortune harms the envious person, but simply because those others have it.
sections.Rhetoric-bound, not clinical: Aristotle specifies that envy targets rivals and near-equals rather than people far above or below oneself — a speaker who wants a jury to feel proprietary hostility toward a successful equal, rather than mere admiration, needs exactly this comparison-to-a-peer framing.
sections.Research note: Aristotle treats phthonos as an unqualifiedly blameworthy pain in the Nicomachean Ethics — unlike nemesis, which can be felt rightly, phthonos has no virtuous mean: it is envy of another's good fortune regardless of whether that fortune is deserved.

metadata.deck: Greek Pathē — Rhetoric and Stoic Ethics

sections.Definition: Rhetoric II.11 defines emulation (zēlos) as a painful desire for goods that people like oneself possess and one lacks — not because the other person has them, but because one wants them too, a pain that moves one to act, not merely to resent.
sections.Rhetoric-bound, not clinical: Aristotle draws the line between zēlos and phthonos on exactly this point of action: emulation spurs a person toward acquiring the good themselves, while envy merely wants the other person to lose it — a distinction useful to a speaker deciding whether to cast an audience's reaction to a rival's success as productive ambition or corrosive resentment.
sections.Research note: Aristotle pairs zēlos with phthonos as the second of the two couples that close Book II's catalogue of pathē (pity/indignation and envy/emulation both concern judgments about the fortunes of others), and separately pairs zēlos with contempt (kataphronesis) as its own contrary in the same closing chapter — briefly discussed there but not developed here as its own item.

sections.Definition: In the Stoic scheme reported by later sources (chiefly Diogenes Laërtius and Stobaeus), lypē is an irrational contraction of the soul at what is wrongly judged to be a present evil. It is one of the four canonical pathē — a mistaken value-judgment about the present, not a physiological given.
sections.Why the Stoics call it irrational: For the Stoics, only virtue and vice are genuinely good or bad; everything else — health, wealth, reputation, even bodily pain — is "indifferent." Lypē arises from judging one of those indifferents to be a real evil. Because the judgment is false, the Stoics hold there is no well-reasoned version of it — unlike the other three pathē, lypē has no eupatheia (rational good-feeling) counterpart in the sage.
sections.Research note: This is an ethical claim about which judgments are true, not a description of a bodily process — reading lypē as equivalent to the modern clinical category "depression," or flattening it to the modern English word "distress," overstates the overlap in both directions.

sections.Definition: Phobos, in the Stoic scheme, is an irrational shrinking-away from an expected evil — the future-facing counterpart to lypē's present-facing contraction. Like the other three pathē it is a judgment: that some coming indifferent is a real evil worth fleeing.
sections.Its rational counterpart: Fear's eupatheia is eulabeia, usually translated "caution" — a well-reasoned aversion to a genuine evil (vice, a wrong action) rather than to an indifferent thing. A Stoic sage, on this account, still avoids stepping off a cliff; the claim concerns which judgment does the avoiding, not the removal of self-preservation.
sections.Research note: The eupatheiai are attributed only to the sage — an ideal the Stoics themselves treat as rarely, if ever, instantiated. This is a normative model of how judgment should work, not a description of how most people's fear does work.

sections.Definition: Epithymia is an irrational reaching-toward a future indifferent, wrongly judged to be a real good — the desire-pole of the Stoic four, paired conceptually with hēdonē (pleasure) the way phobos is paired with lypē: future versus present, in each case built on a mistaken value-judgment.
sections.Its rational counterpart: Epithymia's eupatheia is boulēsis, "wish" or rational will — desire aimed only at what is genuinely worth wanting: wisdom, justice, courage, self-command. The Stoics did not hold that a sage desires nothing; they held that a sage desires correctly.
sections.Research note: Later Stoic sources subdivide epithymia into a long list of named species — anger itself is sometimes classed as a form of it, a desire for revenge. This item covers the genus, not its species.

sections.Definition: Hēdonē is an irrational swelling of the soul at a present indifferent, wrongly judged to be a real good — the present-facing counterpart to epithymia's future reach, and structurally opposite to lypē.
sections.Its rational counterpart: Hēdonē's eupatheia is chara, "joy" — a well-founded elation at something genuinely good, namely virtuous action itself, rather than at an indifferent circumstance. The Stoics distinguish chara sharply from hēdonē: the same felt shape, resting on a different object and a different judgment.
sections.Research note: Later Stoics, especially the Roman Stoic Seneca, develop chara at length as a durable good feeling available regardless of external circumstance — an idea with obvious later influence on Christian and secular therapeutic traditions, none of which this item claims as Stoic in origin.

sections.Definition: Descartes places wonder (admiration) first among the six and treats it as unique: a sudden surprise of the soul that causes it to attend to and consider objects that seem rare or extraordinary — before the soul has judged whether the object is good or bad for it. Wonder is purely cognitive orientation toward novelty; unlike the other five, Descartes says it has no bodily opposite and does not depend on whether the object benefits or harms us.
sections.Why it comes first: Because wonder precedes any judgment of good or evil, Descartes treats it as the passion that makes the other five possible — nothing can become an object of love, hatred, desire, joy, or sadness until it has first been noticed as significant. Excess wonder, in his account, produces astonishment (étonnement), which can freeze a person into inaction; its useful degree he calls generosity of curiosity, a disposition to keep learning.
sections.Research note: This is the clearest point of contrast with basic-emotion models built around universal facial expressions (see the ekman-basic school in this collection): Descartes's wonder is defined by its relationship to prior knowledge (is this new to me?), not by any claimed facial signature.

sections.Definition: Descartes defines love as an agitation of the soul caused by the animal spirits, which impels the soul to join itself willingly to objects that appear agreeable to it — a felt movement toward union with something judged good, whether that something is a person, an object, or an idea.
sections.Its degrees: Descartes distinguishes affection (for something judged inferior to oneself), friendship (for an equal), and devotion (for something judged superior — God, one's country, one's sovereign). He treats these as differences of the same primitive passion rather than as separate ones.
sections.Research note: Descartes explicitly pairs love with hatred as its bodily and functional opposite (both concern union versus separation from an object), which is why they are grouped together in this deck's second-level composite.

sections.Definition: Hatred, in Descartes's scheme, is the mirror of love: an agitation caused by the spirits that impels the soul to will itself separated from objects presented to it as harmful. Where love draws the soul toward union, hatred drives it toward distance and rejection.
sections.Its physiology: Descartes ties hatred's bodily signature to a supposed bitterness in the blood and a tightening around the heart, part of his broader (and now superseded) mechanistic account of how each passion moves the animal spirits differently through the body.
sections.Research note: Descartes's specific physiology — animal spirits, the pineal gland as the soul's seat — is not treated as a live scientific claim by this school; his primitive-passion taxonomy is read independently of the 17th-century mechanics used to explain it.

metadata.image_credit: "Hatred or Jealousy", plate 20 from Heads Representing the Various Passions of the Soul (after Charles Le Brun), British print, 1765 — The Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0 (Open Access).

sections.Definition: Desire is an agitation of the soul, caused by the spirits, that disposes it to will for the future whatever it represents to itself as agreeable — the only one of the six primitive passions Descartes defines as inherently future-facing.
sections.Its scope: Descartes treats desire broadly: it covers wanting to obtain a good one does not yet have and wanting to avoid an evil one fears, and even the desire to preserve a good one already possesses (since preservation is itself a kind of future-directed willing). He does not give desire a named opposite among the six.
sections.Research note: Descartes's desire is closer to what later philosophy calls a conative or motivational state than to a discrete felt emotion — it is defined by what it moves the soul to will, not primarily by how it feels.

metadata.image_credit: "Desire", plate 8 from Heads Representing the Various Passions of the Soul (after Charles Le Brun), British print, 1765 — The Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0 (Open Access).

sections.Definition: Joy is an agreeable emotion of the soul, in which the enjoyment it possesses consists — the felt experience of having, right now, what one has judged to be good. Where desire looks forward and love reaches toward union, joy registers a good already present or already attained.
sections.Its relation to love: Descartes treats joy as frequently accompanying love (one is glad about what one loves) but keeps them conceptually distinct: love is the movement toward union, joy is the register of possession. One can, on his account, love something one does not yet possess, in which case joy is absent and desire dominates instead.
sections.Research note: Descartes pairs joy with sadness as its direct opposite — both concern a good or evil the soul takes to be already present, rather than merely possible.

metadata.image_credit: "Laughter", plate 10 from Heads Representing the Various Passions of the Soul (after Charles Le Brun), British print, 1765 — The Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0 (Open Access). Used for joy (Le Brun's plate is titled by its outward expression, laughter, rather than by Descartes's own term).

sections.Definition: Sadness is a disagreeable languor in which the soul's discomfort consists, arising from an evil, or a lack, that the soul represents to itself as belonging to it now — the counterpart to joy's registration of a present good, this time registering a present evil or absence.
sections.Its relation to hatred: As joy relates to love, sadness relates to hatred: hatred is the movement of rejection toward a harmful object, sadness is the felt discomfort of the evil or lack already being present. Descartes treats prolonged, ungrounded sadness as physiologically corrosive, and recommends attending to genuine present goods as a corrective — an early version of what later therapeutic traditions would call reappraisal.
sections.Research note: Descartes's six close on an opposing pair (joy/sadness) that mirrors the earlier pair (love/hatred), leaving wonder and desire as the two primitives without a named opposite in his own scheme.

metadata.image_credit: "Sadness", plate 13 from Heads Representing the Various Passions of the Soul (after Charles Le Brun), British print, 1765 — The Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0 (Open Access).

sections.Definition: Amor is the first concupiscible passion: a connaturality or fittingness the sensitive appetite feels toward an apprehended good, prior to any movement toward or away from it. Aquinas treats it as the root passion from which desire and joy both follow — one desires what one first loves, and rejoices in possessing what one loves.
sections.The arduousness axis: Amor is concupiscible, not irascible, because it responds to the good simply as good — a fitting object, full stop — without regard to whether attaining or keeping it is difficult. Compare spes (hope), an irascible passion below: hope requires the good to be not just apprehended but hard to reach. Love does not.
sections.Research note: Aquinas distinguishes amor (a passion of the sensitive appetite, shared with animals in an analogous form) from caritas (charity, a theological virtue involving the will and grace) — this item concerns only the passion, not the virtue.

metadata.image_credit: Leaf from a Roman de la Rose manuscript (Guillaume de Lorris's God of Love allegory), mid-14th century — The Walters Art Museum, via Wikimedia Commons, public domain. Roughly a lifetime after Aquinas (d. 1274); used as the closest available Gothic manuscript treatment of amor, not as an illustration of the Summa itself.

sections.Definition: Tristitia is the concupiscible passion of pain at a present evil apprehended as such — the counterpart to gaudium (joy) at a present good. Aquinas distinguishes several species by cause: pity (sorrow at another's evil), envy (sorrow at another's good, treated by Aquinas as a species of sorrow gone wrong), and anxiety (sorrow that weighs down the mind so it cannot see a way out).
sections.The arduousness axis: Tristitia responds to a present evil simply as evil, without regard to whether escaping it is difficult — which is exactly what separates it from timor (fear, an irascible passion, below): fear concerns a future evil that is hard to avoid, while sorrow concerns an evil already here.
sections.Research note: Aquinas holds that tristitia, unlike some passions, can be reduced by four specific remedies he names explicitly: weeping, the sympathy of friends, contemplating truth, and sleep or a bath — a concrete, almost clinical list embedded in an otherwise abstract taxonomy.

sections.Definition: Spes is the irascible passion of the appetite's movement toward a future good that is both possible to attain and arduous — difficult enough that attaining it is not a foregone conclusion. If the good were easy and certain, Aquinas holds, the appetite would simply desire it (a concupiscible act); it becomes spes specifically because obtaining it requires effort or struggle against resistance.
sections.Why the key is transliterated, not \"hop: English "hope" is used loosely for almost any positive expectation, easy or hard. Aquinas's spes is defined by the arduousness condition — no difficulty, no spes, just ordinary desiderium (desire). Keying this item as plain "hope" would erase the one feature that makes it irascible rather than concupiscible in the first place, and would silently merge it with every other school's much broader use of the English word.
sections.Research note: Aquinas pairs spes with desperatio (despair): both concern the same future arduous good, differing only in whether the appetite judges it attainable (spes) or not (desperatio).

sections.Definition: Timor is the irascible passion of shrinking from a future evil that is arduous to avoid — an evil difficult enough to escape that the appetite registers real resistance, not simply distaste. Aquinas catalogues species of timor by their object: laziness (fear of the effort a task requires), shame (fear of disgrace), and others.
sections.Why the key is transliterated, not \"fea: As with spes, the arduousness condition is what makes timor a distinct technical category rather than the everyday English word. An evil that is easy to avoid produces no timor in Aquinas's scheme, only ordinary aversion (fuga, concupiscible). Using plain "fear" as the key would quietly fold that structural distinction back into the very undifferentiated folk category this taxonomy exists to divide.
sections.Research note: Timor's irascible partner is audacia (daring), the passion of confronting rather than fleeing the same arduous evil — not included as its own item in this skeleton.

sections.Definition: Ira is the irascible passion of rising up against a present, arduous evil already inflicted — specifically, the desire to overcome or take revenge upon whoever caused it. Aquinas holds ira alone among the eleven has no contrary passion: there is no separate irascible passion of, say, meek acceptance of a present injury, because the irascible appetite's whole function is to confront arduous evil, and confronting it just is ira.
sections.Why the key is transliterated: Aquinas's ira is narrower than everyday English "anger": it specifically requires a present injury already suffered and a movement toward retribution against its cause — closer to what a modern reader might call righteous or retaliatory anger than to any irritation whatsoever. Keeping the Latin key flags that narrower scope rather than importing the full breadth of the modern word.
sections.Research note: Because ira has no contrary, it sits oddly against the rest of Aquinas's paired structure — commentators have long noted this as a structural asymmetry in the eleven-passion scheme, not an oversight this deck is introducing.

Used for ira as the closest available period image of righteous wrath and violent retribution; not a literal illustration of Aquinas's ira.

sections.Definition: Odium is the concupiscible passion contrary to amor: a disagreement or dissonance the sensitive appetite feels toward an apprehended evil, prior to any movement to avoid or destroy it. Where amor is a connaturality with a good, odium is its exact structural mirror toward an evil.
sections.The arduousness axis: Odium stays concupiscible, not irascible, for the same reason amor does: it responds to the evil simply as evil, without regard to whether resisting or escaping it is difficult. That is what separates it from timor (fear, irascible, above): fear requires the evil to be hard to avoid; hatred does not.
sections.Research note: Aquinas holds, against a more intuitive symmetry, that hatred is not a primary passion parallel to love but always presupposes it: "omne odium ex amore causatur" — every hatred is caused by some love (q. 29, a. 2). One hates an evil only because it opposes a good already loved; love, not hatred, is structurally first.

sections.Definition: Desiderium (also concupiscentia) is the concupiscible passion of movement toward a good not yet possessed. It follows directly from amor — one desires what one already loves — and precedes gaudium: desiderium is the appetite still in motion toward the good; gaudium is the appetite come to rest in it.
sections.The arduousness axis: As with amor, desiderium responds to the good simply as good, apprehended as not-yet-had, without regard to difficulty. This is the exact concupiscible counterpart to spes (hope, irascible, above): spes is what desiderium becomes when attaining the good turns out to require struggle against real resistance. No arduousness, no spes — only desiderium.
sections.Research note: Aquinas distinguishes desiderium of a good simply apprehended from the will's act of intending (intentio) the same object — the passion belongs to the sensitive appetite and is common to humans and animals in analogous form; intentio belongs to the will alone.

sections.Definition: Fuga is the concupiscible passion contrary to desiderium: a shrinking away from an apprehended evil not yet present, prior to any judgment about how hard that evil is to escape. Aquinas states the whole concupiscible scheme in one line: "in concupiscibili sunt tres coniugationes passionum: scilicet amor et odium, desiderium et fuga, gaudium et tristitia" — in the concupiscible faculty there are three pairings: love and hatred, desire and aversion, joy and sorrow (q. 23, a. 4).
sections.Why the key is transliterated, not \"ave: English translations render fuga as "aversion," "dislike," or "flight" fairly interchangeably, which can blur the one distinction that matters here: fuga is the concupiscible response to a future evil considered simply as evil. The moment that same future evil is considered arduous — difficult to escape — the passion is no longer fuga but timor (fear, irascible, above). Aquinas states the boundary explicitly: fear adds to fuga a certain lowness of spirit, on account of the difficulty of shunning the evil.
sections.Research note: Fuga is the least discussed of the six concupiscible passions in the secondary literature relative to its partner desiderium — Aquinas treats it mostly by contrast, defining it against desire and against fear, rather than devoting it an extended discussion of its own species.

sections.Definition: Gaudium (Aquinas also uses delectatio, pleasure/delight, largely interchangeably for the sensitive-appetite case) is the concupiscible passion of the appetite coming to rest in a good actually possessed — the counterpart to tristitia (sorrow, above) at a present evil, and the terminus of the sequence amor–desiderium–gaudium: one loves a good, desires it while absent, and rejoices in it once had.
sections.Distinct from the pair already in this s: This school's first item, amor, already named gaudium as one of the passions following from love; this item gives it its own entry rather than leaving it a passing mention inside amor's. Gaudium and delectatio are not perfectly synonymous for Aquinas — delectatio can apply more broadly to bodily pleasure and gaudium more properly to a rational or willed satisfaction — but at the level of the sensitive-appetite passion this skeleton describes, the two names cover the same concupiscible passion of rest in a possessed good.
sections.Research note: Aquinas devotes several articles (qq. 31–34) to the causes of delectatio — operation, the presence of the good, likeness, hope, sorrow's cessation, and others — a more elaborate treatment than tristitia's shorter remedy-list receives, reflecting his general procedure of treating a passion and its contrary asymmetrically rather than as strict mirror images.

sections.Definition: Desperatio is the irascible passion contrary to spes: a recoil from a future good that is arduous and, unlike spes's object, judged impossible to attain. Both passions concern the identical object — a hard-to-reach future good — differing only in the appetite's judgment of whether reaching it is possible.
sections.Why the key is transliterated, not \"des: English "despair" is used broadly for hopelessness of many kinds, easy or hard, sudden or chronic. Aquinas's desperatio is defined narrowly against the same arduous future good spes targets — it names the specific judgment that a hard-won good is now impossible, not despondency in general. Keying this item as plain "despair" would erase the one feature shared with spes — the arduous object — that makes it a distinct irascible passion rather than a mood.
sections.Research note: Aquinas pairs desperatio with spes as the first couple of the irascible faculty and holds that hope naturally precedes despair in the order of the passions — one must first apprehend a good as attainable, however arduously, before that judgment can reverse into despair (q. 25, a. 3; q. 40).

sections.Definition: Audacia is the irascible passion contrary to timor: a movement toward confronting a future, arduous evil, arising when the appetite judges that evil resistible rather than overwhelming. Where timor shrinks from the arduous evil, audacia rises up against it — the same object, met with the opposite inclination.
sections.Why the key is transliterated, not \"cou: Audacia is a passion of the sensitive appetite, not the intellectual virtue of fortitude — Aquinas treats it as the raw movement toward confronting danger that virtue must then govern and moderate, not as virtue itself. It is also narrower than everyday "daring": it specifically requires the same arduous future evil timor targets. An excess of audacia unchecked by reason is, on this account, rashness rather than courage.
sections.Research note: Aquinas holds anger (ira, above) presupposes audacia: no one seeks revenge without first daring to pursue it, which is part of why ira sits last in the irascible order and, uniquely among the eleven passions, has no contrary of its own.

sections.Definition: Śṛṅgāra is the rasa built from the sthāyibhāva rati (love, romantic attachment). Bharata treats it as arising when a performance's determinants — a beautiful setting, the presence of a beloved, appropriate ornament and gesture — combine with the audience's own capacity to relish that theme, tasted rather than merely witnessed.
sections.An event, not a character's inner state: Śṛṅgāra does not belong to the character on stage (who may be performing convincingly without personally feeling love in that moment) nor simply to the spectator (whose ordinary daily love for a spouse is not itself śṛṅgāra). It is what arises in the relish of a spectator competent to engage with a well-built performance of rati — a three-way relation among craft, convention, and a trained aesthetic response, not a two-way transfer of feeling from actor to viewer.
sections.Research note: Bharata and later theorists (notably Abhinavagupta) subdivide śṛṅgāra into sambhoga (union) and vipralambha (separation) — the rasa of love-in-fulfillment and love-in-longing are treated as two registers of the same rasa, not opposites.

metadata.image_credit: Bangal Ragini, from a Ragamala series, c. 1650, Malwa (Central Indian School) — Smithsonian's National Museum of Asian Art, CC0. Ragamala paintings of this raga are typically about longing for an absent lover, fitting śṛṅgāra's vipralambha (love-in-separation) register.

sections.Definition: Hāsya is the rasa built from the sthāyibhāva hāsa (mirth). The Nāṭyaśāstra treats laughter itself as graded — Bharata catalogues distinct types of laughter by intensity and by whose laughter it is (a refined character's smile differs, dramaturgically, from a low or vulgar character's laugh), and hāsya as a rasa is the audience's relish of that graded comic display, not the display alone.
sections.An event, not a character's inner state: A performance can present hāsa (a character being visibly amused) without producing hāsya in the audience, if the comic timing or convention fails — the rasa is contingent on the craft succeeding, not automatic from the content being nominally funny.
sections.Research note: Bharata pairs hāsya with śṛṅgāra causally in his own account — he holds that hāsya is in fact produced from śṛṅgāra (comedy as a kind of derivative or parody of the romantic), one of several explicit derivation relationships among the eight that this skeleton does not fully trace.

sections.Definition: Karuṇa is the rasa built from the sthāyibhāva śoka (grief, sorrow) — typically arising in performance from separation from loved ones, loss, curse, exile, or the destruction of what is cherished. It is the rasa most often invoked for tragic and elegiac performance across the Sanskrit dramatic tradition.
sections.An event, not a character's inner state: Karuṇa is the audience's aesthetic relish of well-performed śoka, not the raw distress a spectator would feel witnessing an actual death or loss. Classical commentary is explicit that rasa involves a kind of distance or generalization (sādhāraṇīkaraṇa) — the specific, personal edge of real grief is transmuted into a shareable aesthetic theme, which is part of why watching a tragedy can be pleasurable in a way that witnessing real grief is not.
sections.Research note: Bhāmaha and later theorists debate at length whether karuṇa's pleasure is genuine aesthetic pleasure or a paradox requiring separate explanation — a live question inside the tradition itself, not settled by Bharata's original text.

sections.Definition: Raudra is the rasa built from the sthāyibhāva krodha (anger), typically arising from confrontation, insult, betrayal, or battle — associated in the Nāṭyaśāstra with demonic and heroic characters (rākṣasas, and warrior figures in conflict) and with red as its governing color and Rudra as its presiding deity.
sections.An event, not a character's inner state: A performer displaying krodha through prescribed gesture, voice, and stance produces raudra in a spectator capable of relishing that display as craft — the rasa is not the actor's own anger (a trained performer is not actually enraged mid-performance) nor a contagious transfer of rage to the audience, but the aesthetic appreciation of anger skillfully rendered.
sections.Research note: Bharata links several rasa-pairs by claimed derivation; raudra is traditionally paired with vīra (the heroic rasa, not yet its own item in this skeleton) as sharing an active, high-energy register, in contrast to karuṇa's passive one.

sections.Definition: Vīra is the rasa built from the sthāyibhāva utsāha (energy, resolve, or heroic determination), typically arising in performance from combat pursued with steady nerve, generosity given without hesitation, or any difficult undertaking carried through with resolve — the Nāṭyaśāstra treats gaura, a fair gold-white, as its governing colour and Indra as its presiding deity.
sections.An event, not a character's inner state: A performer's display of utsāha — steady gaze, upright carriage, controlled breath and gesture — produces vīra in a spectator equipped to relish that display as craft, not because the audience has itself become heroic or because the actor is personally resolute off-stage. Vīra sits, with raudra, in the Nāṭyaśāstra's active, high-energy register, though the two are built from different determinants: confrontation and insult for raudra, a difficult undertaking pursued with resolve for vīra.
sections.Research note: Later commentators distinguish types of vīra by the kind of resolve involved — dāna-vīra (heroism through unhesitating generosity), dayā-vīra (heroism through compassion sustained under difficulty), and yuddha-vīra (heroism in battle) — a three-way subdivision this skeleton does not develop further.

sections.Definition: Bhayānaka is the rasa built from the sthāyibhāva bhaya (fear), arising in performance from threatening sounds, sights of danger, or the depiction of terrifying beings and situations — a register the Nāṭyaśāstra pairs closely with bībhatsa (disgust) and raudra as its neighboring negative-register rasas.
sections.An event, not a character's inner state: As with the other rasas, bhayānaka names the audience's relish of a well-built fear-display, not the character's or the audience's own visceral terror — a distinction the tradition needs precisely because genuine terror is not, in itself, an aesthetic pleasure, while bhayānaka, tasted at the right remove, is treated as one.
sections.Research note: Bharata's account of bhayānaka's typical determinants (vibhāva) — the sight of frightful forms, the sound of screams, an empty or dark space — reads as a fairly literal stagecraft manual for producing dread, distinct from a psychological theory of what fear itself is.

sections.Definition: Bībhatsa is the rasa built from the sthāyibhāva jugupsā (disgust, aversion, repugnance), arising in performance from the sight of the foul, the decayed, the venomous, or the otherwise repellent — the Nāṭyaśāstra pairs it closely with bhayānaka and raudra as neighboring negative-register rasas, with blue as its governing colour and Mahākāla, a fierce form of Śiva, as its presiding deity.
sections.An event, not a character's inner state: A well-built display of jugupsā — recoil, averted gaze, the described presence of something rotten or venomous — produces bībhatsa in a spectator who can relish that display as craft, at the aesthetic remove that lets repugnance become a source of theatrical interest rather than mere revulsion. As with the other rasas, bībhatsa is not the raw disgust a person would feel encountering the actual foul thing.
sections.Research note: Bharata's account of bībhatsa's determinants (vibhāva) reads largely as a sensory catalogue — decaying flesh, worms, foul smell described in performance — closer in spirit to bhayānaka's stagecraft-manual quality than to karuṇa's more psychologically elaborated grief.

sections.Definition: Adbhuta is the rasa built from the sthāyibhāva vismaya (wonder, astonishment), arising in performance from the sight of the divine, the supernatural, the unexpectedly magnificent, or an event beyond ordinary explanation — with yellow as its governing colour and Brahmā as its presiding deity.
sections.An event, not a character's inner state: Adbhuta names the audience's relish of a well-built display of vismaya — a widened gaze, a suspended gesture, the staged arrival of something marvelous — not a spectator's own naive astonishment at a stage trick; the rasa depends on the display being recognized as craft even while it produces something like wonder in response to it.
sections.Research note: Later commentators subdivide adbhuta by the source of the marvel — wonder at the divine and wonder at ordinary but startling good fortune are treated as different registers of the same rasa, a distinction this skeleton does not develop further.

sections.Definition: Śānta, built from the sthāyibhāva śama (tranquility, or in some formulations the disposition toward liberation), was argued for as a ninth rasa by the 10th–11th century Kashmiri philosopher-aesthetician Abhinavagupta, several centuries after Bharata's original eight. Abhinavagupta treats śānta as, in a sense, the ground state underlying the other eight — the settled awareness from which any of the eight active rasas can arise and to which they return.
sections.A contested addition, argued rather than: Not everyone in the tradition accepted śānta as a rasa. Objectors held that a rasa requires an actively displayed sthāyibhāva — visible in a character's speech, gesture, and situation — while śama is precisely the absence or cessation of active emotional display, making it structurally unlike the other eight. Abhinavagupta's defense (developed at length in his Abhinavabhāratī commentary) is itself part of what makes śānta worth including here: it is a live philosophical argument inside the tradition, not a settled ninth entry Bharata himself endorsed.
sections.Research note: Abhinavagupta's broader philosophical commitments (he was also a major theorist of Kashmir Shaivism) inform his case for śānta — he connects aesthetic relish (rasāsvāda) to a state structurally similar to, though not identical with, spiritual realization (brahmāsvāda-sadṛśa, "resembling the taste of the absolute"), a controversial and much-discussed claim in later Sanskrit aesthetics.

items.name: Xǐ (喜) — Joy, Governed by the Heart

sections.Definition: Xǐ is paired with the heart (xīn) in the classical five-viscera correspondence. In modest degree it is considered healthy — the heart's proper state is described as one of ease and open communication with the world — but the Huangdi Neijing holds that excessive or sudden joy can scatter and slow heart qì, producing symptoms the text describes in terms consistent with what modern readers might call palpitations, restlessness, or difficulty concentrating.
sections.Wider than the English word: Classifying xǐ simply as "happiness" undersells how the classical texts use it: it names a specific quality and direction of qì movement (an outward, expansive, scattering tendency) tied to a specific organ system, not a private felt mood in the modern psychological sense. The pathology is about qì dynamics, not about mood valence as such.
sections.Research note: The claim that a specific emotion in excess damages a specific organ is a theoretical framework internal to classical Chinese medicine, built on the Five Phases (wǔxíng) correspondence system (heart–fire, in this case) rather than on the anatomical or biochemical mechanisms modern cardiology would investigate.

items.name: Nù (怒) — Anger, Governed by the Liver

sections.Definition: Nù is paired with the liver (gān), whose classical function is to ensure the smooth, unobstructed flow of qì throughout the body. Anger is held to cause qì to rise and rush upward and outward — the Neijing associates excessive nù with liver qì stagnation or liver-yang rising, described in symptom-language including headache, a flushed face, and irritability.
sections.Wider than the English word: As with xǐ, nù names a directional qì disturbance (an upward, forceful surge) associated with a specific organ system's proper function being disrupted, not a discrete inner feeling considered on its own. Frustration, resentment, and irritability are often discussed under the same liver-qì framework even where the English words would distinguish them.
sections.Research note: The liver–anger pairing is one of the most frequently cited five-viscera correspondences in both classical sources and contemporary Traditional Chinese Medicine clinical practice, though contemporary TCM's own systematization dates mainly to 20th-century standardization efforts building on, but not identical to, the classical texts.

items.name: Sī (思) — Pensiveness/Overthinking, Governed by the Spleen

sections.Definition: Sī is paired with the spleen (pí), the organ classically responsible for transforming food into qì and blood. Sī names sustained mental concentration, worry, or rumination — Bharata's rasa school and this school share nothing structurally, but sī resembles neither pure "thought" nor pure "emotion" in the English sense: it sits at the seam between the two, which is exactly the kind of category the English word "emotion" does not have room for.
sections.Why this key is transliterated, not \"wo: English forces a choice between a cognitive gloss ("overthinking," "rumination") and an affective one ("worry," "anxiety"), and either choice discards half of what sī names in the source texts: a single qì-disturbing pattern of dwelling on something, cognitively and affectively at once. Picking one English word would silently resolve an ambiguity the classical texts do not resolve.
sections.Research note: The Neijing holds that excessive sī knots spleen qì, impairing its transforming function — described in symptom-language including poor appetite, fatigue, and a bloated or heavy sensation, consistent with the digestive role assigned to the spleen in this system.

items.name: Bēi (悲) — Grief, Governed by the Lung

sections.Definition: Bēi is paired with the lung (fèi), classically responsible for governing qì and respiration. Grief and sorrow are held to disperse or deplete lung qì, and the Neijing associates prolonged bēi with shortness of breath, a sunken or withdrawn bearing, and general depletion of vital energy.
sections.Wider than the English word: Some classical sources pair the lung with yōu (worry, anxious brooding) rather than, or alongside, bēi (grief proper) — the seven-emotion list and the five-viscera list do not map onto each other item-for-item, and different texts group yōu and bēi together under the lung differently. This item follows the more common grief-lung pairing; the worry-lung variant is noted here rather than given its own entry.
sections.Research note: The lung's classical association with grief has an often-cited resonance with the Five Phases correspondence of metal (associated with autumn, decline, and letting go) to the lung — a symbolic-seasonal logic distinct from, and not reducible to, a modern respiratory-physiology account of sadness.

items.name: Kǒng (恐) — Fear, Governed by the Kidney

sections.Definition: Kǒng is paired with the kidney (shèn), classically the organ storing jīng (essence) and considered the root of the body's constitutional reserves. Kǒng is held to cause qì to sink and descend, and prolonged fear is associated in the Neijing with depletion of kidney essence — described in symptom-language including weakness in the low back and knees, and in more severe classical descriptions, loss of bladder control under acute fright.
sections.Wider than the English word: The classical texts distinguish kǒng (a more settled, dwelling fear or apprehension) from jīng (a sudden fright or shock, sometimes counted as a separate seventh emotion, sometimes folded into kǒng depending on the source) — a distinction of duration and suddenness that plain English "fear" does not mark on its own.
sections.Research note: The kidney's role as the body's constitutional root makes fear's association with it medically significant within the system: kidney depletion is treated as a serious, slow-to-recover condition, so chronic kǒng is regarded as a comparatively grave pattern rather than a passing state.

items.name: Yōu (忧) — Worry, Paired with the Lung

sections.Definition: Yōu is the term the classical five-organ correspondence table in Suwen chapter 5 (Yin Yang Ying Xiang Da Lun) itself pairs with the lung (fèi) — not bēi (grief), which this school's existing bēi item already flags as a later variant. Yōu names a settled, anxious brooding or apprehension rather than acute sorrow; the Neijing holds that yōu, sustained, injures lung qì the same way excessive bēi is elsewhere said to.
sections.How it differs from bēi and from sī: Three qīqíng terms sit close together and are worth distinguishing explicitly: bēi is acute grief at a loss, tied to the lung in the wider seven-emotion tradition; sī (this school's existing item) is a spleen-tied cognitive dwelling, closer to rumination; yōu, in the classical five-zhì (五志) table, is the lung's own paired term — a lower-grade, longer-lasting apprehensive worry rather than either sī's mental fixation or bēi's sharper grief. Later Chinese medical writing sometimes uses bēi and yōu together or nearly interchangeably for the lung, which is why this school's bēi item already notes the overlap; this item gives yōu its own entry as the more classically primary of the two lung-paired terms.
sections.Research note: The interaction cycle recorded alongside the five-zhì table states that yōu injures the lung and joy (xǐ) overcomes yōu — part of the same Five Phases control sequence (fire controls metal) that governs how the five organ-emotion pairs are held to check one another.

items.name: Jīng (惊) — Fright, the Sudden Counterpart to Kǒng

sections.Definition: Jīng is the seventh term completing the qīqíng list alongside the five-viscera emotions and yōu — a sudden startle or fright, distinct in the classical texts from kǒng's more settled dread. The Suwen's Ju Tong Lun (chapter 39) states the difference in its own qì-movement vocabulary: kǒng makes qì descend (恐则气下), while jīng throws qì into disorder (惊则气乱) — a different disturbance, not simply a stronger dose of the same one.
sections.Sudden versus sustained — the distinctio: This is the one distinction worth stating plainly, because collapsing jīng into kǒng loses it: jīng is acute and initially unsettles the heart (xīn), which houses shén (spirit/mind) and is disturbed first by any sudden shock, scattering its qì chaotically. Only if the fright is severe or repeated does the disturbance settle into the kidney (shèn) as a more sustained kǒng, depleting the essence the kidney stores. Kǒng, by contrast, is already the sustained, dwelling apprehension this school's existing kǒng item describes — jīng is what a sudden, discrete startle does before it has had time to become that.
sections.Research note: Because jīng is described as unsettling the heart before the kidney, some later commentators treat it as sitting outside the strict five-viscera correspondence altogether — a seventh emotion with a two-organ trajectory rather than a single fixed pairing, which is part of why classical sources vary on whether to count it as its own qíng or as a variant of kǒng.
